units.la: Dversarius noster in Refutatoriis, uti vocat, Dissertationibus, non tam presso pede mecum congredi, quàm captata hinc inde & obtorto collo rapta occasione Theologos nostros Praestantissimos aggredi, eosque miro artificio vel tragicé exagitare, vel suarum facere partium instituit. Hoc nempe ipsi opus, hic labor erat, ut ἔργον faceret, quod erat παρέργον, quò lectoris intentionem & judicium à principali themate, in quo sibi parum confisus est, ad accessoria & heterogenea obliquè pertraheret, adeóque fucum ei faceret. Ego priusquam me accingerem ad modestum examen eorum, quae non unus, sed plures antagonistae adversus unum conspirantes, cum Demetrio Ephesinae Dianae promacho & complicibus πλήρεις θυμῶ, pleni & tumentes excandescentiâ protulerunt, necessum duxi in antecessum diluere ea, quae ab ipso passim in Theologos nostros Clarissimos, extra instituti metas, declamata sunt. Discussò hoc pulvere, quem medio in certamine dolosi luctatoris instar adversus nos excitavit, ut oculorum aciem praestringeret vel obtunderet, deinceps inoffenso pede ad Synodalis nostrae dissertationis justas vindicias progrediemur. Apparebit interim ex brevi etiam hoc ψευγεύματι, qua fide, Helveticáne an Punica, quóve candore famosus hic athleta in arenam nobiscum adeó praeceps descenderit.
units.tr: Our adversary, in what he calls his Refutations, his Dissertations, has not thought fit to meet me face to face, but rather, seizing on any occasion that offers itself and dragging it in by the neck, has set out to attack our most distinguished theologians, either tormenting them with a tragic display or turning them to serve his own party. This, indeed, was his task and his labour: to make a principal matter out of what was only a side matter (ἔργον from παρέργον [work from by-work]), so that he might obliquely draw the reader's attention and judgement away from the main subject, in which he had little confidence, towards incidentals and irrelevancies, and so blind him. Before I set about a modest examination of those things which not one but several antagonists, conspiring against one man, have brought forward, together with Demetrius, champion of Diana of Ephesus, and his fellow-conspirators, full of wrath and swelling with excitement [πλήρεις θυμῶ], I have judged it necessary first to dissolve those charges which he has everywhere hurled against our most distinguished theologians, beyond the limits of the question at hand. Once this dust has been cleared away, which he raised in the middle of the contest like a crafty wrestler to dazzle or dull the sharpness of our sight, we shall proceed with an unhindered step to the just defence of our Synod's dissertation. Meanwhile, it will appear even from this brief lie [ψευγεύματι] with what good faith, Swiss or Punic, and with what candour, this notorious athlete has so rashly entered the arena against us.

units.la: II. Institutum tantum non palmarium adversarij est, me Ecclesiae meae Doctoribus confodere. Ita loquitur pag. 194. Et pag. 180. haec in verba infit: Num quid Evangelium, quod tali & aliis pluribus (quas Johannes Georgius Rhaetus in sua face veritatis Rat.6. coacervat) contradictionibus constat, potest esse verum Christi Evangelium? Praepostere id nobis occinit adversarius. Fides quippe nostra aliud, idque inconcussum magis habet fundamentum Verbi Dei & propriae conscientiæ sensui, non multorum consensui innititur. Esto igitur, magni Ecclesiæ nostræ Doctores, οἱ διδάσκαλοι σύλοι εἶναι, alicubi á Pontificiis steterint partibus, piámque adeó causam deserue-rint. At nos nostrum faciemus illud, quod olim Josua apud populum Israelis ingeminavit: Quòd si malum videtur in oculis vestris colere Dominum: at ego & familia mea colemus Dominum, Jos. 24:15. Nostra faciemus verba Tertulliani lib. de Præscriptionibus pag. m. 96. Quid ergo, si Episcopus, si Diaconus, si vidua, si virgo, si Doctor, si etiam Martyr lapsus á regula fuerit, ideó hæreses veritatem videbuntur obtinere? Ex personis probamus fidem, an ex fide personas? Nemo sapiens est nisi fidelis, nemo major, nemo Christianus; nemo autem Christianus, nisi qui ad finem usque perseveraverit. Tum in propatulo sunt nostræ Confessiones, aliáque scripta symbolica, quibus externa nostra unio & in fide consensio innititur. Hæc sibi probè probéque constant. Ultima primis, & media utrisque examussim respondent. Nulli in ijs cothurni, nulla oraculo Delphica. Præterea sanctè profiteri & in Domino gloriari possumus, in fundamento fidei, & nominatim etiam eâ doctrinâ Evangelicâ, quam adversus Papatum defendimus, summam per Dei gratiam inter Theologos nostros á veritate adversus mendacium unanimiter stantes, esse voluntatum, studiorum & sententiarum consensionem. Georgium Rhætum in futilissima sua Face (de qua fortassis Redingio nostro canere licuit: Hos ego versiculos feci, tulit alter honores) diffensum nobis impingentem, efficaciter, quod strenuè dissimulat noster, retudit & in ordinem redegit Vir Clarissimus, Jacobus Vedrosius, Ecclesiæ Curiensis Decanus meritissimus. Eandem labem nobis denuo objectam procedente hac disputatione abstergere Σ. Θ. conabimur.
units.tr: II. The adversary's aim, almost his trump card, is to stab me with the teachers of my own Church. So he speaks on p. 194. And on p. 180 he opens with these words: Can the Gospel, which is marked by such and many other contradictions (which John George Rhaetus heaps up in his Torch of Truth, Rat. 6), be the true Gospel of Christ? The adversary sings this to us out of tune. Our faith rests on a foundation that is more secure and unshaken: the Word of God and the sense of our own conscience, not the agreement of many. Granted, then, that our great teachers of the Church (οἱ διδάσκαλοι σύλοι εἶναι [the teachers were wicked]) have at some point sided with the Papists and deserted the pious cause. We will make our own the words Joshua once repeated before the people of Israel: But if it seems evil in your eyes to serve the Lord, then I and my house will serve the Lord, Josh. 24:15. We will also take up the words of Tertullian, in his book On Prescription, p. 96: What then, if a bishop, a deacon, a widow, a virgin, a teacher, or even a martyr has fallen from the rule, will heresies on that account seem to hold the truth? Do we prove the faith from persons, or persons from the faith? No one is wise except the faithful, no one greater, no one a Christian; and no one is a Christian who has not persevered to the end. Moreover, our Confessions lie open to all, and the other symbolic writings, on which our outward union and agreement in faith rest. These are consistent with themselves, properly and honestly: the last answers to the first, and the middle to both, exactly. There is no buskin in them, no Delphic oracle. Besides, we may solemnly profess and boast in the Lord that, among our theologians, standing with the truth against falsehood, there is a unanimous agreement of wills, studies and opinions on the foundation of the faith, and especially on that evangelical doctrine which we defend against the Papacy. Georgius Rhaetus, in his most frivolous Torch (about which perhaps our Redingius might sing: I made these little verses, another took the honours), who has charged us with dissent, has been effectively driven back and brought into order by that most distinguished man, James Vedrosius, most worthy Dean of the Church of Chur. We shall try, in the course of this disputation, to wipe off this same stain, now thrown at us again.

units.la: III. Quòd si nunc telum isthoc in adversarium retorquere luberet, bone, quam fœcunda seges cum eo ludendi se nobis offerret! Numquid enim cum Bellarmino aliisque notam Ecclesiæ facit consensum in doctrina fidei cum capite, & membrorum inter se? Adeò ut Ecclesiæ Pontificiæ veræ Ecclesiæ axioma minimè constet, nisi ejus membra cum capite & inter se consentiant. Atqui quis nisi imprudens ignarúsque rerum omnium concordiam eorum discordem, & littora littoribus contraria, fluctibus undas ignorat? Non umbratici Doctores, sed antesignani; nec antesignani duntaxat, sed Ordines; nec Ordines duntaxat, sed Ordinum conglobatæ sectæ adversus se indivicem infesta signa ferunt. Neque adeò de lana caprina vel umbra suberis, sed maximi momenti articulis, puta de Regula fidei, potestate Papæ, prædestinatione, peccato originali, Gratia, arbitrio, alijsque primarijs capitibus, contentio est. Bellarminus plus quàm trecentas variantes suorum gregalium, Cadmæorum Fratrum, sententias enarrat. In ipso Concilio Tridentino vix ullum dogma stabilitum est, quin gravissimos in medio consessu adversarios prius expertum fuerit, uti Concilij ejus historia á Patre Paulo descripta, quæ a adversarijs aperta veritatis vi sauciatis est, quod ajunt, sudes in oculis, plenissimam fidem facit. Hoc adeò verum est, ut præstare ausim Theologiæ Reformatæ Systema aliquod, ex verbis totidem tum diversorum Doctorum Pontificiorum, veritati instar Bileami testimonium perhibentium, tum Juris Canonici, contextum. Tanta videlicet vis est veritatis, ut teste Lactantio, ex invitis etiam pectoribus erumpat. Nempe Deus aliquando in gratiam Ecclesiæ facit, ut Ægyptij stent adversus Ægyptios, Esa. 19:2. Bellum enim hæreticorum est pax Ecclesiæ, uti verissimè pronunciatum Hilario de Trinitate lib. 7. Sed age, ordine descendamus ad singula objectæ dissensionis nostræ capita.
units.tr: III. But if I wished to turn this weapon back against my adversary, good heavens, what a fruitful field would offer itself for sport! For does not Bellarmine, along with others, make agreement in doctrine of the head with the members, and of the members among themselves, a mark of the Church? So much so that the axiom of the Papist Church, that it is the true Church, does not hold unless its members agree with the head and with one another. Yet who, unless he were foolish and ignorant of all things, would not know that their agreement is discord, and that shores are opposed to shores, waves to waves? They are not mere shadowy teachers but standard-bearers; nor are they only standard-bearers, but whole ranks; and not only ranks, but sects formed of ranks, carry hostile standards against one another. And the dispute is not about trifles, nor about goat's wool or the shadow of cork, but about articles of the greatest weight: the rule of faith, the power of the Pope, predestination, original sin, grace, free will, and other primary heads. Bellarmine recounts more than three hundred differing opinions of his own fellows, the brothers sprung from Cadmus' teeth. In the Council of Trent there was hardly any dogma established without first having met the most serious adversaries in the midst of the assembly, as the history of that Council written by Father Paul shows fully, a history in which, as they say, the Papists' eyes have been wounded by the open force of truth, a stake in the eye. This is so true that I would venture to set out a system of Reformed theology, woven from the words of as many diverse Papist teachers, who, like Balaam, bear witness to the truth, and also from the Canon Law. So great is the power of truth that, as Lactantius testifies, it breaks forth even from unwilling breasts. Indeed God sometimes, for the sake of his Church, causes Egyptians to stand against Egyptians, Isa. 19:2. For the war of heretics is the peace of the Church, as very truly said by Hilary, On the Trinity, book 7. But come, let us descend in order to the individual heads of the dissent objected to us.

units.la: IV. Primó Evangelicos inter se, tum etiam de dissensu eorum, qui Lutheranorum nomine perperam á nobis discernuntur, Zwinglium & Bullingerum, quorum memoria est in benedictione, cum Beza & Hottingero, sanctæ itidem recordationis Theologis, committere conatur pag. 17. 123. & 172. Illos nempe Lutheri de corporis Christi in Eucharistia præsentia dogma traduxisse tanquam Antichristianum, Eutychianum, Nestorianum, monstrosum, absurdissimum. Hos vero dissensum hunc elevasse, adeo quidem ut Hottingerus in ultima Synodali dissertatione exisdimaverit, quaestionem illam esse in materia adiaphora, cujusque ad credendum licentiae relinquendam. Primo adversarius, qui suos in hoc ulcere ungues habet, meminisse debebat, funestae illius Evangelicos inter de coena Domini dissensionis culpam ipsosmet Papistas sustinere. Fluxit enim ex eorum transubstantiatione, tanquam putidissima sententia, ex qua Lutherus in caeteris satis perspicax, emergere penitus non potuit. Tum de Christi in coena Domini praesentia inter nos minime controvertitur. De modo praesentiae tota disceptatio est, quae ad fundamenti fidei ac salutis summam haud refert. Praesentem esse Christum in Coena Domini fatemur utrinque. Fuffi sunt Collocutores Lipsiaci. Quoad modum praesentiae, in eo etiam consensus est, mysticum & sacramentalem esse. Caeterum in eo dissensus totus est: An corpus Christi praesens secundum indistantiam loci, organo oris comedatur a dignis & indignis? Hoc ita negamus, ut ultro tamen fateamur, errorem cum in se, non in consectariis nec agnitis ab adversa parte nec confessis, spectatum, non trabis sed festucae rationem habere & stipulae, quae in examine & probatione nostri, in legitimo coenae Dominicae usu, protinus exuritur & evanescit. Hic porro dissensus noster ludus & jocus est, si comparetur cum Scholasticorum circa Eucharistiam, acerrimis certaminibus. De quibus nobis testis esse potest ipse Redingius, adeo in Scholasticorum Sophistica subactus, ut & Theologiam Scholasticam ipse conscripserit, & ad Scholasticum ejusmodi & Philosophicum praelium me, ut cum barbaro fierem barbarus, animose citaverit. Dominicanorum & Franciscanorum, quorum illi productivam, hi in instanti adductivam in Coena Domini mutationem urgent, obortam in Concilio Tridentino συρρᾶξιν luculenter describit Historicus lib. IV. pag. 295. 296. Sententiarum circa Transubstantiationis Helenæ Pontificiæ dogma, divortia in nostris ad Sess. XIII. Concilij Tridentini quæstionibus Theologicis,etiam nos exponimus.
units.tr: IV. First, he tries to set the Evangelicals against one another, and to bring into question the disagreement of those whom we wrongly distinguish under the name of Lutherans: Zwingli and Bullinger, whose memory is blessed, along with Beza and Hottinger, theologians of holy memory, on pp. 17, 123 and 172. He claims that they condemned Luther's doctrine of the presence of Christ's body in the Eucharist as Antichristian, Eutychian, Nestorian, monstrous, most absurd. And that Hottinger in his last Synodal dissertation raised this disagreement to such a degree that he thought the question was one of an indifferent matter, to be left to the liberty of each to believe as he pleases. But first, the adversary, who has his claws in this sore, ought to remember that the Papists themselves bear the blame for that deadly dissension among the Evangelicals about the Lord's Supper. For it flowed from their transubstantiation, as a most rotten opinion, from which Luther, otherwise sharp enough, could not escape at all. Moreover, there is no real controversy among us about the presence of Christ in the Lord's Supper. The whole dispute is about the mode of presence, which does not much affect the sum of the foundation of faith and salvation. We both confess that Christ is present in the Lord's Supper. The Colloquy of Leipzig was a failure. As to the mode of presence, there is agreement here too: that it is mystical and sacramental. Otherwise the dissent lies entirely in this: Is the body of Christ, present according to the non-distance of place, eaten by the mouth's organ by the worthy and the unworthy? We deny this, while nonetheless freely granting that the error, if it is considered in itself and not in its consequences, which were neither acknowledged nor confessed by the other side, has the character of a splinter and not a beam, and of stubble, which in the examination and proof of ourselves, in the lawful use of the Lord's Supper, is at once burnt up and vanishes. Our dissent here is indeed a game and a jest, if it is compared with the most bitter contests of the Scholastics about the Eucharist. Redingius himself can be a witness to these, so thoroughly was he trained in Scholastic sophistry that he has himself written a Scholastic Theology, and has boldly summoned me to such a Scholastic and philosophical battle, so that I might become a barbarian with the barbarian. The Dominicans and Franciscans, of whom the former urge a productive change in the Lord's Supper, the latter an instantaneous, bringing-about change, and the clash that arose between them at the Council of Trent, is clearly described by the historian in book 4, pp. 295 and 296. We ourselves also set out, in our theological questions on Session 13 of the Council of Trent, the divergences of opinion concerning the dogma of transubstantiation, the Papist Helena.

units.la: V. Sed Zwinglius ipse & Bullingerus,inquit ille,de Lutheranorum illo dogmate non idem sentiunt cum Beza & Hottingero. Primò si quis inter eos dissensus est, manifestum est, non in doctrina ipsa, sed in judicio de doctrinæ momento consistere. Deinde Poëtam agis, Redingi. De Zwinglio allegas testem Scultetum Annal. ad A. C. 1525. ubi ne hilum quidem eam in rem extat. Constat satis, Zwinglium nihil unquam in Lutherum dixisse inclementius. Dextram fraternitatis Marpurgi Cattorum ipsi obtulit. Et quomodo erga ipsum animatus fuerit, epistola ad ipsum A.1527. exarata, & publici juris facta ostendit. Bullingerus, fateor, adversus Brentium Theologorum Heidelbergensium de nova doctrina Ubiquitaria allegat judicium, quo statuitur, eam ex Christo fingere hominem plane Eutychianum. De Flacianis loquuntur Theologi illi, non veris Lutheranis. Neque tam de doctrina confessa, quàm confessæ doctrinæ consequentijs. Errare Lutheranos,inprimis Ubiquitarios graviter,nunquam negârunt nostri. At in fundamentum fidei arietare illos, qui Lutheri doctrinam simpliciter tenent, rectè inficiatur Beza,eúmque secutus Cl. Hottingerus, quibus vetustiores Theologi minimè adversantur. Constat enim, eos Lutheri expetijsse amicitiam, nunquam expetituri,si fundamentum fidei ab illo concussum & eversum credidissent. Quòd verò Cl. Hottingero tribuit,in ultima Synodali disputatione ipsum quæstionem eam venditâsse pro adiaphora, cujúsque ad credendum licentiæ expósita, ad eandem singendi pertinet licentiam, quam ipsa disputatio illa,verè Cygnea Viri Summi cantio, lecta validè refutat. units.tr: V. But, he says, Zwingli himself and Bullinger do not think the same as Beza and Hottinger about that dogma of the Lutherans. First, if there is any disagreement between them, it is plain that it lies not in the doctrine itself but in the judgment about how important the doctrine is. Next, you are playing the poet, Reding. As your witness about Zwingli you cite Scultetus, Annals, at the year 1525, where there is not the slightest trace of that matter. It is quite certain that Zwingli never said anything more unkind about Luther. At Marburg, in Hessian territory, he offered him the right hand of brotherhood. And the spirit in which he regarded him is shown by the letter he wrote to him in 1527 and made public. Bullinger, I admit, in his reply to Brenz, the Heidelberg theologians, on the new Ubiquitarian doctrine, cites a judgment by which it is declared that it fashions from Christ a man wholly Eutychian. Those theologians speak of the Flacians, not of the true Lutherans. Nor do they speak so much of the doctrine professed as of the consequences drawn from the professed doctrine. Our people have never denied that the Lutherans err, especially the Ubiquitarians, and err gravely. But that those who simply hold Luther's doctrine batter the foundation of faith is rightly denied by Beza, and by the distinguished Hottinger who follows him, and the older theologians by no means oppose them. For it is established that they sought Luther's friendship, and would never have sought it had they believed that the foundation of faith had been shaken and overthrown by him. As for what he ascribes to the distinguished Hottinger, that in the last synodal disputation he sold that question as a thing indifferent, and exposed to a license for believing, it belongs to the same license of invention, which that disputation, truly the swan song of that most eminent man, refutes strongly when it is read. In thesis 16 I read these words: The Lutherans press such a presence of the body in the Lord's Supper as repugns all of Holy Scripture, the analogy of faith, purer antiquity, and sober reason, which we are not at all ashamed of. Is this what it means to hold that question as a thing indifferent, exposed to a license for believing?

units.la: Zwinglius & Bullingerus an circa Lutheranorum de Eucharistia dogma diversum sentiant à Beza & Hottingero? ad credendam licentiae exposita? Adiaphorum enim quod est, ejus materia nec verbo Dei, nec fidei analogia, nec puriori antiquitate, nec sobria ratione omnino definita est.
units.tr: Do Zwingli and Bullinger hold a different view from Beza and Hottinger about the Lutherans' doctrine of the Eucharist? Exposed to a license for believing? For a thing indifferent is one whose matter is in no way defined either by the Word of God, or by the analogy of faith, or by purer antiquity, or by sober reason.

units.la: VI. De distinctione Pontificijs usitata inter cultum duliae, hyperduliae & latriae, solicitat adversarius Zwinglium, Calvinum, Bezam & Molinaeum, tanquam confitentes reos, quod ea Patribus probata fuerit, pag. 24. & 193. De cultu hyperduliae audax & perfrictum hoc Redingij commentum est. Neque enim de eo unum jota nostrates Theologi. Norunt exacte, hyperduliae vocem, & rem ipsam voce significatam esse non ἄγραφον duntaxat, sed etiam ἀπαράδοτον, nuper demum inventam, & veteribus omnibus incognitam. quod de voce ipse Bellarminus non dissimulat, qui proinde statuit, Ecclesiae posteriori hic licuisse ὀνοματοποιεῖν, hoc est, καινοτομεῖν. Verum sive vocem hyperduliae, sive rem spectes, nihil ea absurdius, nihil blasphemum magis. Dulia & in Scripturis, & apud vetustissimos Christianos est religiosus Dei Optimi maximi cultus. Ergo qui hyperduliam B. virgini vendicant, ij ex Divini quidem & veteris Ecclesiastici sermonis usu, ei cultum tribuunt eo ipso, qui Dei est, superiorem. Quoad cultus duliae & latriae distinctionem, eam vel Patribus promiscue usitatam esse, vel sensu Pontificio usitatam esse, nemo unquam nostrum fassus est. Zwinglius in Epicherefi allegata ab adversario, ejus nc quidem meminit. Alibi, nimirum Explanat. artic. 20. graviter refutat. Calvinus Instit. l. 1 2:2. inter alia habet: At complures ex Patribus hac distinctione usi sunt. Quid tum, si omnes eam perspiciunt non modo impropriam esse, sed penitus frivolam? Respondet strictim & κατὰ συγχώρησιν, non directe. Patere igitur, Redingi, quomodo res habeat, te edoceri paucis. Latriae illa & duliae distinctio vestro explicata sensu, non tantum a verbo Dei est longe alienissima, sed a cana etiam Antiquitate. Beatissima illa & vere Christiana tria priora Secula nullo discrimine, veluti a Christi nomine & grege alienos habuerunt, quicunque ulli omnino rei praeter solum Deum cultum sive duliae sive latriae impenderent. Neque alius in tanta librorum veterum numero locus occurrit, qui vel hanc vel aliam consimilem cultus religiosi vel divisionem vel distinctionem doceat. Id post alios nuper admodum liquidissimé demonstravit Cl. Dallæus De religiosi cultus objecto lib. 1. cap. 5.6. ad quem adversarium nostrum amandamus. Primus Augustinus duliæ & latriæ distinctionem posuit, duliam interpretatus eam servitutem, secundum quam Apostolus servos suis Dominis subditos esse debere præcipit, adeóque non religiosum, sed civilem cultum, societatis nimirum erga Sanctos superstites, dilectionis erga defunctos. Post Homerum mihi scribendæ forent iliades, si loca Augustini eó facientia apponere instituerem. Videsis Chamierum, illum Pontificiorum malleum, De cultu creaturarum cap. 8.
units.tr: VI. The adversary attacks Zwingli, Calvin, Beza and Molinaeus, as if they were guilty parties who confessed, because the distinction commonly used by the Papists between the cult of dulia, hyperdulia and latria was approved by the Fathers, p. 24 and 193. This is Reding's bold and brazen fiction about the cult of hyperdulia. For our theologians know exactly that the word hyperdulia, and the thing signified by the word, is not only unwritten [ἄγραφον] but also undelivered [ἀπαράδοτον], a thing only recently invented and unknown to all the ancients. Bellarmine himself does not hide this about the word, and therefore he holds that the later Church was permitted to coin names [ὀνοματοποιεῖν], that is, to make innovations [καινοτομεῖν]. But whether you look at the word hyperdulia or at the thing, nothing is more absurd, nothing more blasphemous. Dulia, both in the Scriptures and among the most ancient Christians, is the religious worship of God, the best and greatest. Therefore those who claim hyperdulia for the Blessed Virgin, by the very use of the divine and the old ecclesiastical language, attribute to her a cult that is superior to that which belongs to God. As for the distinction between the cult of dulia and of latria, no one of ours has ever admitted that it was either used indiscriminately by the Fathers or used in the Papist sense. Zwingli, in the Epicheiresis cited by the adversary, does not even mention it. Elsewhere, namely in the Explanation of Article 20, he refutes it severely. Calvin, Institutes book 1, chapter 12, section 2, among other things says: But several of the Fathers used this distinction. What of it, if all of them see that it is not only improper but utterly frivolous? He answers briefly and by way of concession, not directly. So, Reding, let it be shown in a few words how matters stand, so that you may be taught. That distinction of latria and dulia, as you explain it, is not only most alien to the Word of God, but also to the hoary antiquity. Those most blessed and truly Christian first three centuries held without any distinction, as if they were aliens from the name and flock of Christ, all who devoted any cult, whether of dulia or of latria, to anything at all besides God alone. Nor does any other passage occur in so great a number of ancient books that teaches either this or any other similar division or distinction of religious worship. This was most clearly demonstrated recently, after others, by the distinguished Dallaeus, On the Object of Religious Worship, book 1, chapters 5 and 6, to whom we send our adversary. Augustine was the first to set up the distinction between dulia and latria, interpreting dulia as that servitude by which the Apostle orders servants to be subject to their masters, and therefore not religious but civil worship, of fellowship toward the saints who survive, namely, and of love toward the dead. If I were to set out the passages of Augustine that bear on this, I would have to write Iliads after Homer. See Chamier, that hammer of the Papists, On the Cult of Creatures, chapter 8.

units.la: VII. Intercessiones Sanctorum, Deiparæ præsertim virgi- nis, à veteribus Ecclesiæ Doctoribus probatas fuisse, testimonijs Zwinglij, Bezæ & Molinæi astruere conatur, pag. 34.
units.tr: VII. He tries to show, by the testimonies of Zwingli, Beza and Molinaeus, that the intercessions of the saints, especially of the Virgin Mother of God, were approved by the ancient teachers of the Church, p. 34.

units.la: Quid verò, Redingi, talis confessio vobis proficeret? Largiamur tamen, Sanctos cœlites virtute communionis & charitatis fraternæ Deo Ecclesiæ militantis statum, quem luctuosum esse haud ignorant, precibus suis commendare; an ideo effici posset, nostros esse illos apud Deum Mediatores, atque eo nomine invocandos esse, vel Regnorum, Provinciarum, Urbium, Pagorum, Templorum, clauストrorum, arcium, &c. tutelarem curam, pro arbitrio hominis Itali, ijs committendam esse? Numquid enim etiam homines vivi pro vivis apud Deum intercedere non debent? An iccirco vivorum illorum apud Deum sunt mediatores? Is mediator est, Redingi, ac proinde invocandus, qui orat primò non tantùm in genere pro omnibus, sed etiam pro singulis, omnibúsque singulorum, quas compertas habere potest, necessitatibus: secundò qui orat non simpliciter, sed ex vi suorum meritorum. Hæc solius Christi dos & prærogativa est. Qui alijs vendicant, sacrilegi sunt. Ii ipsi Patres, qui de intercessione Sanctorum loquuntur, eos tamen tanquam Mediatores nostros invocandos esse, nusquam scisc unt. Jam de Theologis
units.tr: But what, Reding, would such a confession profit you? Let us grant that the heavenly saints, through the power of communion and fraternal charity, commend to God the state of the Church militant, which they know to be sorrowful. Could it therefore follow that they are our mediators with God and are to be invoked under that name, or that the care of guardianship over kingdoms, provinces, cities, villages, temples, cloisters, citadels and so on is to be entrusted to them at the whim of an Italian? For do not living men also ought to intercede with God for the living? Are those living men therefore mediators with God? He is a mediator, Reding, and therefore to be invoked, who prays, first, not only in general for all but also for individuals, and for all the needs of individuals that he can know of; and second, who prays not simply but by virtue of his own merits. This is the sole dowry and prerogative of Christ. Those who claim it for others are sacrilegious. Those very Fathers who speak of the intercession of the saints nowhere know that they are to be invoked as our mediators. Now, as for our theologians...

units.la: Intercessiones Sanctorum à veteribus probatas esse, an docent nostri? logis nostris. Zwinglius in Epicherefi pag. m. 181. hæc verba habet: Temporis diuturnitatem, quam unam velut Achillis scutum obiectant, & Hieronymi contra Vigilantium amara potius quàm firma tela, nihil moror. Nos enim Christum ex suis verbis non ita didicimus. Fides nostra alium sub pallium non admittit. Lectulus enim nimis angustus est. Teneo eum, nec dimittam. Aurea verba. Diuturnitatem obiectari tanquam Achillis scutum ait. Quàm verè, non dicit, nec quam temporis diuturnitatem illis concedat, exprimit. Beza loco citato nihil habet. Molinæus concedit, veteres alicubi de intercessione sanctorum loqui. Quomodo se res habeat, dispiciendum. Ante Cypriani ætatem nullum omnino extat traditionis hujus vestigium. Fatetur ipse Perefius de Tradit. p. 3. confid. 7. Cypriani & eum consequente ætate distingui oportet sententias privatas à publica doctrina Ecclesiæ. Privati affectus privata quædam judicia protuserunt: quæ, ut fit, paulatim latiùs vagata, tandem doctrinæ publicæ faciem induerunt, donec se undique confirmaret stabiliretq; hagiolatria. Quoad Cyprianum, allegari solet Epistola ejus 57. in qua tamen de particulari cura nullum verbum, sed tantùm de generali dilectione & oratione pro fratribus & sororibus. Irenæus lib. 4:19. Mariam vocat advocatam Evæ, viventem puta adhuc in terris, non regnantem in Cœlis: non quód pro ea sive precibus sive meritis suis intercesserit apud Deum, sed quia peperit filium Dei, in quo solo Eua salvata est. Advocatam vocat significatu tum temporis recepto, quo advocare idem erat quod consolari, advocatio idem quod consolatio, adeóque advocatus consolator. Quod observatum pridem non tantùm nostratibus, Chamiero, Mathæo Bacharto, & nuper Cl. Dallæo de religiosi cultus objecto pag. 44 45: sed etiam ipso Rigaltio Notis ad Tertull. de Patient. Cap. 11. ad pag. 166. Quæ citant deinceps, longè sunt recentiora & ultra Seculum tertium, ut Gregorij Nazianzeni, Hieronymi, Augustini, Leonis. Quædam etiam hypobolimæa sunt, velut ea, quæ recitantur ex meditationibus Augustini, e Liturgijs, & Athanasij sermone in Evangelium de Deipara.
units.tr: Do our theologians teach that the intercessions of the saints were approved by the ancients? Zwingli, in his Epicheiresis, p. 181, has these words: I take no account of the length of time, which they throw up as Achilles' shield, nor of Jerome's bitter rather than firm weapons against Vigilantius. For we have not learned Christ in that way from his words. Our faith does not admit another under its cloak. For the bed is too narrow. I hold him and will not let him go. Golden words. He says that the length of time is thrown up as Achilles' shield, but he does not say whether it is correct, nor does he express how much length of time he grants them. Beza, in the passage cited, has nothing. Molinaeus concedes that the ancients somewhere speak of the intercession of the saints. How the matter stands must be examined. Before the age of Cyprian there is no trace at all of this tradition. Perefius himself admits, de Tradit. p. 3, confid. 7, that one must distinguish, from the age of Cyprian and those who followed him, private opinions from the public doctrine of the Church. Private affections produced private judgments, which, as usually happens, gradually spread more widely and at last took on the face of public doctrine, until hagiolatry confirmed itself on every side and became stable. As for Cyprian, his Epistle 57 is usually cited, yet in it there is no word about particular care, only about general love and prayer for brothers and sisters. Irenaeus, book 4:19, calls Mary advocate of Eve, supposing her still living on earth, not reigning in heaven: not because she interceded with God for her by prayers or merits, but because she bore the Son of God, in whom alone Eve was saved. He calls her advocate in the sense then current, when advocare meant the same as to console, and advocatio the same as consolation, and so advocatus meant consoler. This was noted long ago, not only by our own people, Chamier, Matthaeus Bachart, and more recently the distinguished Dallaeus, de religiosi cultus objecto, pp. 44–45, but also by Rigaltius himself, Notes on Tertullian, de Patientia, ch. 11, at p. 166. The later authorities they cite afterwards are far more recent and go beyond the third century, such as Gregory Nazianzen, Jerome, Augustine and Leo. Some are even spurious, such as those passages quoted from Augustine's Meditations, from the liturgies, and from Athanasius' sermon on the Gospel concerning the Mother of God.

units.la: VIII. In Zwinglium & Bezam, quos heterodoxos Novatores appellat homo ἑτεροδοξώτατος, qui doctrinam sequitur Tridentino Concilio non antiquiorum, graviter invehitur pag.41.114. & 209. Crimini illis dat, quòd profiteantur, se nihil morari S. Hieronymum, utpote idololatriæ defensorem in eo,quòd contra Vigilantium Sanctorum invocationem probet. Hos meos Magistros me imitari vociferatur. Unum agnosco διδάσκαλον καὶ καθηγητὴν Magistrum & ductorem, Christum. Zwinglium & Bezam sequor,quia sub unius ejusdemque Magistri, Christi nimirum signis contra Antichristum militant. Cæterum Zwinglij de Hieronymi amaris potius quàm firmis telis verba sapientissima superiùs posui. Ait, se non ita Christum ex suis verbis didicisse. Negat fidem nostram alium sub pallium suum admittere. Lectulum nimis angustum esse asserit. Quàm veré hoc scripserit, apparebit, si Hieronymum cum Vigilantio contenderimus. Epistola 13. ad Paulinum, Vigilantium Barchinomensum Presbyterum, Sanctum vocavit. At postquam is se reliquiarum cultui oppositi, & damnavit circumgestationem pulveris, lampadas ad sepulchra, & pervigilia, in eum acerbissimè invehi & detonare occœpit. Quem priùs Sanctum appellaverat, nunc vocat cauponem Calagurritanum, stirpe latronum prognatum, Judæum, Samaritanum, canem viventem & rabidum, Dormitantium, eructantem immundissimam crapulam, & qui solus velit adorari. Suum adversus Vigilantium scriptum inauspicato sic orditur: Multa in Urbe monstra generata sunt. Centauros & Sirenas, ululas & onocratalos in Esaja Legimus. Job Leviathan & Behemoth mystico sermone describit. Cerberum & stymphalidas, aprumque Erimanthium & Leonem Nemæum, chimaram atque hydram multorum capitum narrant Fabulæ Poetarum. Cacum describit Vergilius. Triformem Geryonem Hispaniæ prodiderunt. Sola Gallia monstra non habuit. Exortus
units.tr: VIII. He bitterly rails against Zwingli and Beza, whom this most heterodox man [ἑτεροδοξώτατος] calls heterodox innovators, pp. 41, 114 and 209, for following a doctrine that is not older than the Council of Trent. He charges them with professing that they have no regard for St Jerome, as a defender of idolatry in that he proves, against Vigilantius, the invocation of the saints. He shouts that I imitate these my masters. I acknowledge one teacher and guide [διδάσκαλον καὶ καθηγητήν], Christ, the Master and leader. I follow Zwingli and Beza because they fight under the banners of one and the same Master, namely Christ, against Antichrist. Moreover, I have set out above Zwingli's very wise words on Jerome's bitter rather than firm weapons. He says that he has not learned Christ in that way from Jerome's words. He denies that our faith admits another under its own cloak. He declares that the bed is too narrow. How truly he wrote this will appear if we set Jerome against Vigilantius. In Epistle 13 to Paulinus, Jerome called Vigilantius the presbyter of Barcelona a saint. But after he opposed the cult of relics and condemned the carrying about of dust, the lamps at tombs and the all-night vigils, Jerome began to rail at him very bitterly and to thunder against him. Him whom he had earlier called a saint, he now calls an innkeeper of Calahorra, sprung from a race of brigands, a Jew, a Samaritan, a rabid living dog, a sleeper, a belcher of the filthiest gluttony, one who alone wants to be worshipped. He begins his own work against Vigilantius with an ill omen in this way: Many monsters have been born in the city. In Isaiah we read of centaurs and sirens, owls and onocrotals. Job describes Leviathan and Behemoth in mystical language. The fables of the poets tell of Cerberus and the Stymphalian birds, the Erymanthian boar and the Nemean lion, the Chimaera and the many-headed Hydra. Virgil describes Cacus. They have related that Geryon of three forms was in Spain. Only Gaul had no monsters. Vigilantius suddenly arose, or rather Dormitantius, etc.

units.la: Hieronymi adversus Vigilantium convitia. tus est subito Vigilantius seu potius Dormitantius &c. Redingi, an putas, Hieronymum ita Christum ex verbis suis didicisse? Quàm procul hæc à stylo Apostolico absunt! Sanè ipse Erasmus, magnus Hieronymi admirator, tractatui Hieronymi talem præfixit censuram: Hieronymus in Vigilantium ita debacchatur, ut plusculum modestiæ in eo cogar desiderare. Quòd si tamen adeò Hieronymus, quem cæteroquin & nos quantivis facimus, adversario placet, & displicet Vigilantius, meminerit sanè, Hieronymum non tantum crimem adorationis Martyrum & reliquiarum studiosissimè diluere, sed etiam Pervigilia in Basilicis Sanctorum unicè commendare. Annon igitur Ecclesia Papistica Hieronymum deserit in eo, quòd Sanctos & martyres adorat, & Vigilantij ipsius in castra transfivit hactenus, quòd vigilias nocturnas, nomine duntaxat superstite, uti rectè etiam Erasmus observat, sustulit? Abrogatis enim nocturnis vigilijs, gliscente spurcitie & multiplicatis scandalis, jejunatum est pridie diei cujusque festi, retento vocabulo vigiliarum. Id ipsum in Vigilantio damnavit Hieronymus. Hæc tu, Redingi, pro tua ἀγχινοία concilia, &, si potes, insuper ostende, ea ætate Vigilantium ab aliis quàm Hieronymo pro hæretico habitum esse? Sanè Augustinus & Theodoretus Hieronymo posteriores texuerunt catalogum hæreticorum ad sua usque tempora. Vigilantium tamen in numerum hæreticorum neutter retulit. Dicit equidem Hieronymus, Vigilantij hærefin à Tertulliano fuisse oppugnatam in Scorpiaco, vel Scorpiace, ut apud Rigaltium ex MS. Codicibus legitur. Liber extat adhuc, scriptus contra Gnosticos & Valentinianos, omnesque Martyriorum refragatores. Adversus horum scorpionum venena theriacam stylo temperavit Tertullianus. Quid hoc ad Vigilantium, quem Gnosticum vel martyriorum fuisse refragatorem nemo dixit? Sed fuerit talis Vigilantius. Cum eo eatenus constitutum nihil omnino haberemus, imò ei anathema promptissimi diceremus. Non enim contra martyria, sed contractum Martyrum disputamus.
units.tr: ...arose suddenly, Vigilantius, or rather Dormitantius, etc. Reding, do you think that Jerome learned Christ in this way from his own words? How far these things are from the apostolic style! Indeed Erasmus himself, a great admirer of Jerome, prefixed to Jerome's treatise this judgment: Jerome rages against Vigilantius in such a way that I am forced to miss a good deal of moderation in him. But if, however, Jerome, whom in other respects we too value highly, is pleasing to your opponent and Vigilantius displeases him, let him certainly remember that Jerome not only most diligently refuted the charge of adoring martyrs and relics, but also most strongly commended the all-night vigils in the basilicas of the saints. Does not the Papist Church therefore desert Jerome in this, that it adores saints and martyrs, and hitherto has gone over to the camp of Vigilantius himself, in that it has abolished the nightly vigils, keeping only the name, as Erasmus also rightly observes? For once the nightly vigils were abolished and filth grew and scandals multiplied, fasting was observed on the day before each feast, the name of vigils being retained. Jerome condemned this very thing in Vigilantius. Reding, you may make of this what your quick wit [ἀγχινοία] suggests, and, if you can, show further that in that age Vigilantius was regarded as a heretic by others than Jerome? Indeed Augustine and Theodoret, writing after Jerome, drew up catalogues of heretics down to their own times. Yet neither of them placed Vigilantius among the heretics. Jerome does indeed say that the heresy of Vigilantius was attacked by Tertullian in his Scorpiacus, or Scorpiace, as is read in Rigaltius from the manuscript codices. The book still survives, written against the Gnostics and Valentinians, and all opponents of the martyrs. Tertullian tempered his pen as an antidote against the venom of these scorpions. What has this to do with Vigilantius, whom no one has called a Gnostic or an opponent of the martyrs? But let Vigilantius be such a man. Even so, we would not hold anything at all settled about him on that ground; indeed we would most readily call him accursed. For we do not dispute against martyrdoms, but against the contempt of martyrs.

units.la: IX. Ecclesiam Tigurinam insectatur Sophista, quòd in Eucharistia cum suo Magistro Zwinglio veritatem traxerit ad Figuram, pag. 44.45. Ut quid ergo, ita concludit, Ecclesia Tigurina sine mandato Dei transtulit veritatem in figuram? O bone, quis te ferat ita declamantem? Vestra haec culpa est. Vos ex eucharistia immani errore veritatem suffulistis. Annon enim comica quadam licentia panem & corpus Christi ex Eucharistia exterminastis, nuda pro pane accidentia substituistis, & sub inani accidentium illorum larva non corpus Christi, sed substantiam quandam indivisibilem & ἀόρατον, corpus non corpus, id est, Nihilum sub Nihilo jam dudum ostentastis & adorandum propositistis? Perinde ac sispectatoribus & communicantibus vestris missaticis ludicrum illud occinueretis: Λαβὲ μηδὲν καὶ κράτει καλῶς: Accipe nihil & tene bene. Vos in hoc ipso mysterio tremendo, veritate sublata, luditis figuris audacibus & inverecundis, quibus Rhetorica nomen nullum dedit. In verbis HOC EST CORPUS MEUM pronomen Hoc vobis denotat rem indeterminatam & vagam. Nihil enim denotat certi, adeóque demonstrat Nihil. Cùm Evangelistae dicunt, Christum panem dedisse, panis vobis carnem denotat. Fructus vitis vobis est sanguis. Hoc facere, vobis est, corpus Christi realiter in sacrificium propitiatorium sacrificare. Corpus Christi dicitis figuratè panem appellari, quia panis fuit ante consecrationem. Perinde ac si diceretis, senem esse Juvenem, quia Juvenis aliquando fuit. Denique omnes vestri de Eucharistia sermones sunt merè figurati & inauditis tropis luxuriantes. Tu ergo, Redingi, Cùm tua pervideas oculis mala lippus inunctis, Cur in amicorum vitijs, tam cernis acutùm, Quàm aut aquila aut serpens Epidaurius? Quomodo verò Ecclesia Tigurina veritatem transtulit in figuram? Fatetur enim & invictis hactenus argumentis demonstrat, panem esse corporis Christi figuram, sed non talem, quae nudè figuret & adumbret rem alienam & ad nos non pertinentem, sed quae in legitimo usu Christum ejusque universa beneficia credenti significet, obsignet & exhibeat. Cum nudis signis, sine nucleo corticibus nihil nobis rei est. Christi ejusque corporis & sanguinis praesentiam quoad modum praesentiae tum relativum seu Sacramentalem, tum Spiritualem consistere, & ad salutarem coenae dominicae usum sufficere debere, si maxime illum praesentiae per contactum localem seu ἀδιαςαςίαν modum, utpote a verbo Dei, Sacramentorum natura & veteris Ecclesiae sensu abhorrentem repudiemus, toties totiesque liquido veritati dedimus. Numquid enim Fideles V.T. in Sacramentis suis Christum non habuerunt praesentem? Sane Agnus ille Dei, qui tollit peccata mundi, jam inde a jactis mundi fundamentis mactatus fuit, Dei videlicet decreto, & Spiritus S. fideique efficacia, Joh. 1:29. Apoc. 13:8. Et V.T. Patres eandem nobiscum Spiritualem escam comederunt, de eadem petra Christo biberunt, 1. Cor. 10:3,4,5. Act. 15:11. Heb. 13:8. An vero ἀσύγατος ille praesentiae corporis Christi localis & inclusivae modus jam tum locum habere potuit? Vides ergo, Redingi, veritatem praesentiae constare posse, etiamsi modus ille praesentiae, quem Sophistice vestra invexit, minime admittatur, & verbi Divini penetrantissimo gladio juguletur.
units.tr: IX. The sophist attacks the Zurich Church because, together with its teacher Zwingli, it transferred the truth into a figure in the Eucharist, pp. 44–45. Why then, he concludes, did the Zurich Church, without God's command, transfer the truth into a figure? Good sir, who could bear you declaiming like this? This fault is yours. You propped up the truth by your monstrous error about the Eucharist. Did you not, with a comic license, banish the bread and the body of Christ from the Eucharist, substitute bare accidents for bread, and under the empty mask of those accidents display long ago, and propose for adoration, not the body of Christ but some indivisible and invisible substance, a body that is not a body, that is, Nothing under Nothing? It is as if you were chanting that ridiculous song to your spectators and to your Mass-communicants: [Λαβὲ μηδὲν καὶ κράτει καλῶς], Take nothing and hold it well. In this very awe-inspiring mystery you play, with the truth removed, with bold and shameless figures, to which rhetoric has given no name. In the words THIS IS MY BODY, the pronoun this denotes for you a thing indeterminate and vague. For it denotes nothing certain, and so points to Nothing. When the Evangelists say that Christ gave bread, bread denotes for you flesh. The fruit of the vine is for you blood. To do this is for you to sacrifice the body of Christ really in a propitiatory sacrifice. You say that the body of Christ is figuratively called bread because it was bread before consecration. It is as if you said that an old man is a youth because he once was a youth. Finally, all your sermons on the Eucharist are purely figurative and run riot in unheard-of tropes. So, Reding, While with bleary eyes you anoint your own faults, why do you see so sharply the faults of your friends, as keenly as an eagle or the serpent of Epidaurus? But how did the Zurich Church transfer the truth into a figure? For it acknowledges, and up to now has demonstrated by invincible arguments, that the bread is a figure of the body of Christ, but not such a figure as merely signifies and shadows a thing alien and not pertaining to us, but one which, in lawful use, signifies, seals and exhibits Christ and all his benefits to the believer. Bare signs, without the kernel of the shell, are nothing to us. The presence of Christ and of his body and blood, as to the mode of presence, consists both in a relative, or sacramental, and in a spiritual way, and must suffice for the saving use of the Lord's Supper. Even if we reject that mode of presence by local contact, or [ἀδιαστασία], as abhorrent from the Word of God, from the nature of the sacraments and from the sense of the ancient Church, we have many times and again given clear witness to the truth. For did the faithful of the Old Testament not have Christ present in their sacraments? Indeed that Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world, was slain from the foundation of the world, by God's decree and by the efficacy of the Holy Spirit and of faith, John 1:29; Rev. 13:8. And the Fathers of the Old Testament ate the same spiritual food with us and drank of the same rock, which was Christ, 1 Cor. 10:3, 4, 5; Acts 15:11; Heb. 13:8. But could that [ἀσύγατος] mode of local and circumscribed presence of the body of Christ have already had a place then? You see therefore, Reding, that the truth of the presence can stand, even if that mode of presence which your sophistry has introduced is in no way admitted, and is slain by the most piercing sword of the Word of God.

units.la: X. Missae sacrificium extitisse in Ecclesia veteri, confitentes Zwinglium, Bullingerum, Calvinum, imo ipsam Confessionem Helveticam adducit adversarius pag. 49.84. & 160. Videamus fidem & candorem hominis. Confessio Helvetica cap. 21. haec verba habet ab adversario indigetata: Missa quae aliquando apud veteres fuerit, tolerabilis an intolerabilis, modo non disputamus. En, qualis fuerit apud veteres missa, non disputat Confessio. Audaculus tamen ille nescio qua consequentiae trochlea infert, Confessionem Helveticam allegatis verbis fateri, veterem Ecclesiam credidisse, missam esse verum & proprie dictum sacrificium. Cogor apud te, Redingi, frontem & pudorem desiderare. Missae veterum meminit Confessio,
units.tr: X. The adversary cites Zwingli, Bullinger, Calvin, and even the Helvetic Confession itself (pp. 49, 84, and 160) to show that the sacrifice of the Mass existed in the ancient Church. Let us look at this man's honesty and candour. Chapter 21 of the Helvetic Confession has the words that the adversary has dragged in: Whether the Mass, as it once existed among the ancients, was tolerable or intolerable, we do not now dispute. Here is what the Confession says about the Mass of the ancients: it does not dispute it. Yet that bold fellow, by some twisted chain of reasoning, infers from these words that the Confession admits that the ancient Church believed the Mass to be a true and properly so-called sacrifice. Reding, I am compelled to say that you lack both shame and a sense of decency. The Confession does mention the Mass of the ancients,

units.la: An Confessio Helvetica, Zwinglius, Bullingerus, Calvinus fateantur, in veteri Ecclesia Missae sacrificium extitisse? fio, hoc est, Eucharistiæ, non theatrici & sacrificialis illius lusus, qui veræ Eucharistiæ vicem apud vos fungitur, & ad veri sacramenti derisionem potiùs quàm honorem pertinet. Notissimum est etenim, veteribus, non tamen ante Ambrosium & Augustinum, eucharistiam venisse nomine Missæ. Qui quidem vocis usus post tempora Augustini adeò increbuit, ut viri docti, Julianus Interpres Novellarum Justiniani, Paulus Diaconus, Auctor historiæ miscellæ, alij plures vocabula Græca συνάγειν & σύναξις per dictionem missæ exprimerent. Neque nos de voce controversiam moveremus, si de re ipsa cum adversarijs conveniret. Pergamus ad Zwinglium. Ex ejus Epicheresi probat, veteres oblationem à Christi morte distinctam agnovisse. Verum est, agnovisse. Sed errorem huncce Patrum ita castigat pag. 183. Errori Patrum occasionem dedit verbi Dei neglectio. Nam si hoc solum velut unicum scopum spectâssent, Eucharistiam nunquam erant aliter appellaturi quàm Christus, quàm Paulus, qui commemorationem, qui testamentum adpellárunt. Ita taxat errorem Patrum in appellatione Eucharistiæ verbum Dei negligentium, ut tamen mox subijciat, nonnullos etiamsi oblationem vocaverint, non aliud tamen putavisse quàm rememorationem esse. Hos inter numerat Chrysostomum, & sic concludit: Unde conjectare licet, priscos illos oblationem vocâsse, quemadmodum nos resurrectionem & natalium Christi diem etiamnum appellamus, non quòd Christus nunc nascatur vel resurgat, sed cum semel hoc factum sit, nomen tamen ad vividiorem memoriam tenemus. Sic & hic quoque factum videri potest. Hæc Zwinglij verba oportebat te, Redingi, lectori etiam repræsentare. Sed fraudem tuam noluisti pellucere. De Patrum hac sententia Zwinglius consentientem habet ipsum Lombardum lib.4. Dist. 12. ubi ait: Illud quod offertur & consecratur à sacerdote, vocari à Patribus sacrificium & oblationem, quia repræsentatio est & memoria sacrificij, & sanctæ immolationis factæ in ara crucis. Atque eo sensu Patribus Eucharistiam venire nominibus ἀναφο- ρᾶς ἐᾶς, θεοσφοφᾶς, τελετῆς, θυσίας, ἱεραρχίας, sacrificij, immola-tionis, oblationis &c. jam pridem ex ipsis Patribus probatum dedit Polyhistor noster Hospinianus Histor. Sacram, lib.2:9. In Bullingeri allegato loco Decad. 5. Serm.9. mirâ astutiâ homo noster sermonem hypotheticum convertit in categoricum. Si veteres, verba Bullingeri sunt, sentiunt cœnam esse sacrificium, & hanc pro refrigerio animorum defunctorum offerendam, non recipimus eorum sententiam, utpote Scripturis non congruam. Calvinus ter in sententiam hanc falso citatur. Loca enim allegata vel plane non extant, vel præsens argumentum ne uno quidem apice attingunt. Alibi, nimirum Instit.4:18.10. hæc verba Redingio e diametro oppositá lego: Utuntur quidem Patres illi sacrificij vocabulo. Verum simul exponunt, se aliud nihil intelligere quam memoriam veri illius & unici sacrificij, quod in cruce peregit Christus unicus, ut ipsi possim prædicant, noster sacerdos.
units.tr: Do the Helvetic Confession, Zwingli, Bullinger and Calvin admit that a sacrifice of the Mass existed in the ancient Church? I reply: yes, that is, of the Eucharist, not of that theatrical and sacrificial game which performs the role of the true Eucharist among you, and which serves to mock the true sacrament rather than to honour it. It is well known that the Eucharist came to be called by the name Mass by the ancients, though not before Ambrose and Augustine. Indeed this use of the word became so common after Augustine's time that learned men, Julian the interpreter of Justinian's Novels, Paul the Deacon, the author of the Historia Miscella, and many others, rendered the Greek words synagein [συνάγειν] and synaxis [σύναξις] by the term missa. We would not quarrel over the word, if the adversary agreed with us about the thing itself. Let us go on to Zwingli. From his Epichereses he proves that the ancients recognised an offering distinct from the death of Christ. True, they did recognise it. But Zwingli rebukes this error of the Fathers thus, on p. 183: The neglect of the Word of God gave occasion to the error of the Fathers. For if they had looked only to this as their single aim, they would never have called the Eucharist anything other than Christ and Paul called it, namely a remembrance and a testament. So he censures the Fathers' error, which was negligence of the Word of God in naming the Eucharist, yet he immediately adds that some, even though they called it an offering, thought it to be nothing other than a remembrance. He counts Chrysostom among these, and concludes thus: From this we may conjecture that those early writers called it an offering, just as we still call the resurrection and the birthday of Christ by their names, not because Christ is now born or rises again, but because, once this has happened, we keep the name for a more lively memory. So may it seem to have been done here too. You ought, Reding, to have set these words of Zwingli before your reader as well. But you did not want your deceit to come to light. On this opinion of the Fathers Zwingli has in agreement the Lombard himself, Book 4, Dist. 12, where he says: What is offered and consecrated by the priest is called by the Fathers a sacrifice and an offering, because it is a representation and a memorial of the sacrifice and of the holy immolation made on the altar of the cross. And in this sense our learned Hospinian has already shown from the Fathers themselves that they called the Eucharist by the names anaphora [ἀναφορά], theophoria [θεοφορία], telete [τελετή], thysia [θυσία], hierarchia [ἱεραρχία], sacrifice, immolation, oblation, etc., in his Historia Sacramentaria, Book 2, ch. 9. In the passage of Bullinger you cite, Decad. 5, Sermon 9, our man has, with remarkable cunning, turned a hypothetical statement into a categorical one. Bullinger's words are: If the ancients think the supper to be a sacrifice, and that it must be offered for the relief of the souls of the dead, we do not accept their opinion, as it is not in agreement with the Scriptures. Calvin is falsely cited three times for this opinion. The passages cited either do not exist at all, or do not touch the present question even by a hair's breadth. Elsewhere, namely Institutes 4.18.10, I read words that are directly opposed to Reding's claim: Those Fathers indeed use the word sacrifice. But at the same time they explain that they understand nothing else by it than the memorial of that true and only sacrifice which Christ, the only one, accomplished on the cross, so that he alone may be our priest.

units.la: XI. Novam nunc confessionem Theologis nostris, B- ullingero, Calvino, Melanchthoni, Breitingero, Kekermanno, Danzio, velut in equuleo extorquere conatur pag.52.84.87.
units.tr: XI. He now tries to extort, as it were on the rack, a new confession from our theologians: Bullinger, Calvin, Melanchthon, Breitinger, Kekermann, Danzius (pp. 52, 84, 87).

units.la: Scribit enim, eos cogi fateri, primis trecentis & quingentis, imo sexcentis à Christo annis viguisse in Patribus sinceram inviolatámque fidei doctrinam, ita ut vera, pia & erudita illorum seculorum antiquitas in SS. Patrum scriptis hodieque conservata, sit habenda pro certa fidei regula. Hoc principio veluti largiter sibi concessô fretus, magna hinc inde fiducia provocat ad quinque sexve primorum seculorum Patres, quorum testimonia nasi instar cerei torquet & inflectit. Atque hic denuo crassum & τετράπηχυ adversarij nostri mendacium vide. Prædictis Theologis nostris tribuit, quod sentiant, piam antiquitatem habendam esse pro certa fidei regula. Hoc nemo illorum dixit, nemini in mentem, ne per somnium quidem, venit. Commendant illi & prædicant veterem, & nominatim etiam Romanam Ecclesiam. Sed nulli profecto dissimulant, quin hodierna Ecclesia Romana degeneraverit à veteri, adeóque sit generosissimi vini pessimum acetum, auri purissimi inanis scoria, ex civitate fideli facta meretrix. Veterem Ecclesiæ Romanæ Catholicismum restitui ab hodiernis Romanensibus flagrantissimè cupit Ven. Breitingerus noster ὁ μακαρίτης, per quem Deus Ecclesiæ nostræ benedixit. Ei se adhæsurum bona fide recipit. Idem votum nostrum est, eadem pollicitatio. Sed annon idem Breitingerus eodem de sectis aureolo libello pag. m. 31. solum Dei verbum agnoscit unicam, perfectam, veram & perspicuam regulam eorum, quæ ad salutem credere & facere refert. ? Annon aperte negat, in gratiam cujuscunque tandem hominis nos adoptare id, quod vel repugnat verbo Dei, vel in eo traditum non est ? Hoccine est piam antiquitatem habere pro regula fidei ? Annon particulares unius vel diversorum temporum Ecclesiæ ἰσότιμον πίστιν λαχεῖν, ejusdem fidei esse participes possunt ? An iccirco una alteram consentientem agnoscit pro regula fidei ? Nimium nimiumque, Redingi, tuus te calculus fallit. Bullingerus l.c. nimirum Decad. 5. Serm. 1. agnoscit, successionem Pastorum certam in primitiva Ecclesia magni momenti fuisse. Sed subijcit ea, quæ tu & Georgius tuus, quia ad palatum non erant, subdole dissimulastis, verba: Quales autem fuerint Pastores à seculis multis, quos Romanæ Ecclesiæ Pastores appellavit Cardinalium, Episcoporum mitratorum & sophistarum vulgus, nemo nescit, nisi sensu communi carens. Ut igitur paucis rem expediamus, fatemur utique, venerandam esse piam & canam antiquitatem, ejusque in fide ὁμόνοιαν, sed ita tamen, ne verbi Divini, quo unicus fidei nostræ canon continetur, eminentissimæ authoritati quidquam derogetur, & nævi, quibus aliquando vel tota Ecclesia, vel eminentes in ea Doctores, salvo interim fidei fundamento, laborârunt, non adoptentur, sed potiùs ex verbo Dei modestè & ἐπεικῶς improbentur. Sententiam nostram paucis expressit Confessio Helvetica cap. 2. Non aspernamur Sanctorum Patrum interpretationes, neq; reprobamus eorundem disputationes ac tractationes rerum cum scripturis consentientes: à quibus tamen recedimus modeste, quando aliena à Scripturis aut his contraria afferre deprehenduntur. Et graviter Calvinus Præfat. Instit. ad Regem Galliæ: Sic in Patrum scriptis versamur, ut semper meminerimus, omnia nostra esse, quæ nobis serviant non dominentur: nos autem unius Christi, cui per omnia, sine exceptione parendum sit. Quód veró eorum interpretamenta fidei nostræ esse regulam negamus, argumentis inducimur gravissimis, quæ nervosissimè collegit Cl. Dallæus libro De usu & abusu Patrum, quibus cum nemo hactenus Pontificiorum congredi sustinuit.
units.tr: For he writes that they are forced to admit that within the first three, five hundred, or even six hundred years after Christ, the pure and inviolate doctrine of the faith flourished among the Fathers, so that the true, pious and learned antiquity of those centuries, preserved to this day in the writings of the holy Fathers, is to be held as a certain rule of faith. Relying on this principle, as if it had been granted him in full, he boldly calls upon the Fathers of the first five or six centuries, and twists and bends their testimonies like a wax nose. Here again see the thick, four-cubit lie [τετράπηχυ] of our adversary. He attributes to the theologians I have named the view that pious antiquity is to be held as a certain rule of faith. None of them ever said this, and it never entered anyone's mind, not even in a dream. They commend and extol antiquity, and the Roman Church by name too. But none of them, surely, conceals the fact that the present Roman Church has degenerated from the ancient one, and so has become the worst vinegar of the finest wine, the empty dross of the purest gold, a faithful city turned into a harlot. Our venerable Breitinger, blessed [ὁ μακαρίτης] be he, through whom God has blessed our Church, ardently desired that the ancient Catholicism of the Roman Church be restored by the present Romanists. Reding takes it that he would cling to that in good faith. It is also our wish and our promise. But does this same Breitinger, in his little golden book On Sects, p. 31, acknowledge only the Word of God as the one, perfect, true and clear rule of what we are to believe and do for salvation? Does he not plainly deny that we should adopt, for the favour of any man whatever, what either contradicts the Word of God or is not taught in it? Is this to hold pious antiquity as a rule of faith? Can particular churches of one or of various times not obtain equal honour of faith [ἰσότιμον πίστιν λαχεῖν], and be partakers of the same faith? Or does one church therefore acknowledge another, agreeing with it, as a rule of faith? Reding, your reckoning deceives you far too much. Bullinger, in the same place, Decad. 5, Sermon 1, acknowledges that a certain succession of ministers was of great importance in the primitive Church. But he adds the words which you and your Georgius craftily passed over, because they did not suit your taste: As for what kind of ministers they were for many ages, whom the cardinals, the mitred bishops and the rabble of sophists called the ministers of the Roman Church, no one is unaware, unless he lacks common sense. So, to settle the matter briefly: we freely admit that the pious and chaste antiquity is to be revered, and its harmony [ὁμόνοιαν] in the faith; but in such a way that nothing is taken from the most eminent authority of the Word of God, by which the sole canon of our faith is contained, and that the blemishes which at times either the whole Church or its eminent teachers laboured under, while the foundation of faith remained safe, are not adopted but rather are disapproved from the Word of God, modestly and moderately [ἐπεικῶς]. Our view is briefly expressed in chapter 2 of the Helvetic Confession: We do not despise the interpretations of the holy Fathers, nor do we reject their disputations and treatments of matters that agree with the Scriptures; yet we depart from them with modesty when they are found to bring forward things foreign to the Scriptures or contrary to them. And Calvin gravely says in the Preface to the Institutes addressed to the King of France: We so handle the writings of the Fathers that we always remember that all things are ours, which serve us, not rule over us; but we belong to the one Christ alone, to whom we must obey in all things without exception. As for our denial that their interpretations are the rule of our faith, we are led to it by very weighty arguments, which the learned Dallaeus has most vigorously gathered in his book On the Use and Abuse of the Fathers, and against which none of the Papists has so far been willing to engage.

units.la: XII. Nunc familiaritatem etiam cum Diabolo intercessisse Zwinglio, Calvino ac Luthero probare satagit pag.82. Miror & stupeo tuam, Redingi, temeritatem. Annon metuisti, ne contumelia tuâ irritatus, regererem multa non ab hostibus confiċta, sed domi vestræ nata & consignata, unde constaret, plurimos Pontifices, Clericos & Religiosos, Monachos inprimis & Moniales Diabolo usosesse vel familiari, vel Magistro? Exorcistis vestris annon tanta cum eo quotidie necessitudo intercedit, ut pœne colludere videantur? Neque enim aliam ob causam tot apud vos obsessi Sathanæ fiunt ludibrium, quám quia is dulci eo consortio trahitur. Quod per Dei ineftabilem gratiam in Ecclesijs nostris non accidit. Jesuita Delrio abstinere non potuit, quin multas magiæ suspeċtas in Papatu grassantes nobis proderet non tantùm formulas, ceremonias, actiones, sed & periculosas opiniones multorum Canonistarum, Legistarum, Theologorum, puta Aureoli, Briansoni, Remigij, Angeli de Clavasio; inprimis de Exorcismo Episcopi Laufannensis, & libello Exorcistico Levini Crucij, & altero Felicis Malleoli. Quid dicam de Pontificibus Silvestro II. Gregorio VII. Benedicto IX. Johanno XIII. Sergio IV. &c. qui magiæ cultores, ejusdem interventu in cathedram Petri successerunt? De seculo XI. sic habet Fasciculus Temporum: Tempus effœminatum incipit circa annum D. 1000. in quo fides Christiana valde cœpit deficere. Augurijs & maleficijs inintendebant, & erat sacerdos sicut populus. Ex sacro ordine veneficos & magos plures memorat Delrio Disquisit. Magic. lib. 2. q. 30. puta Johannem Teutonicum Canonicum Halberstadiensum, Monachum illum, qui in gratiam Ducis Aureliani incantabat Regem Carolum, Palumbum Presbyterum necromanticum potentem Romæ, Dominicanos Bernæ exustus, alios. Marinus Mersennus Minorita Parisiensis, Philosophus & Theologus famosissimus, veneficij & magiæ accusat Georgium Venetum, nec non Archangelum Burg. Contra ipsum Mersennum Diabolicam magiam palam scriptis suis docere, Gaffarellus & ipse hoc crimine infamis non minore spiritu contendit. Pontificios amuletis & Periaptis fidere more Gentilium & Judæorum, Nicolaus Remigius & ipse Papista Dæmonol. lib. III. 3. fatetur. Quid dicam de mirionibus & Thaumaturgis, qui revelationes à Diabolo expetierunt? Eremitarum, Hieronis Monachi, Valentis Monachi exempla produxit Cornelius à Lapide in Comment. ad 2. Cor. 11:15. Plura hinc inde recitant Metaphrastes, Cæsarius, Cantipratensis, Discipulus, Lipomannus, Surius, alij. Notissimus est Petrus Cottonus Jesuita, magus decantatissimus, qui ex Diabolo inter decurias aliquot quæstionum petebat: Quo dicto Scripturæ probari potest purgatorium? Quid circa honores mearum reliquiarum? Quid de vita Regis? Quid circa Genevæ conservationem, circa Genevensium plagiarium Deus me vult scire? Ita Hermolaus Barbarus, Patriarcha Aquilegiensis, teste Joh. Baptista Monlorio, impostorem dæmonem consuluit, quid esset Aristotelis entelechia? Si quis attente legerit nupera Exorcistarum scripta, ut Monachi Michaelis historiam Ludovici Gaufridi & obsessarum mulierum, non satis mirari poterit impietatem & stoliditatem hominum, qui Judicium controversiarum fidei à dæmonibus exposcunt, eos singunt pœnitentiæ prædicatores, eos adigunt, ut preces ad Deum fundant, & omnia religionis & pietatis externa munia obeant. Taceo ejusmodi plurima, quæ ad totius Christianismi infamiam pertinent. Vides interim, Redingi, tutiús longè imposterum te facturum, si ab ejusmodi maledictis abstineas, & post totopprobria vestra, cum Scævæ filijs lateas. Nimiúm premendo alienas nares, proprium sanguinem elicis.
units.tr: XII. Now he tries to prove that Zwingli, Calvin and Luther also had familiarity with the Devil (p. 82). I marvel and am astonished at your rashness, Redinger. Did you not fear that, provoked by your insult, I would reply with many things not invented by enemies but born and attested in your own house, from which it would be plain that many Pontiffs, clerics and religious, monks above all and nuns, have made use of the Devil as a familiar or a master? Is there not such daily intimacy between your exorcists and him that they seem almost to be playing together? For there is no other reason why so many of the possessed among you become the sport of Satan, than that he is drawn in by that sweet fellowship. This does not happen in our churches, by God's ineffable grace. The Jesuit Delrio could not refrain from disclosing to us many suspect magical practices flourishing in Popery: not only formulas, ceremonies and actions, but also the dangerous opinions of many canonists, lawyers and theologians, namely Aureolus, Briançon, Remigius and Angelus de Clavasio, above all concerning the exorcism of the Bishop of Lausanne, the exorcistic booklet of Levinus Crucius, and another by Felix Malleolus. What shall I say of the Pontiffs Silvester II, Gregory VII, Benedict IX, John XIII, Sergius IV, and others, who were cultivators of magic and by its agency succeeded to the chair of Peter? Concerning the eleventh century the Fasciculus Temporum says this: "An effeminate age began about the year of our Lord 1000, in which the Christian faith began greatly to fail. They devoted themselves to auguries and evil arts, and the priest was just like the people." From the sacred order Delrio records several poisoners and magicians, namely Johannes Teutonicus, canon of Halberstadt, that monk who in favour of the Duke of Orleans cast spells over King Charles; Palumbus, a presbyter and powerful necromancer at Rome; Dominicans at Bern who were burned; and others. Marin Mersenne, a Paris Minorite, a philosopher and theologian of great fame, accuses Georgius Venetus, and also Archangelus of Burgos, of poisoning and magic. Against Mersenne himself, Gaffarel, himself also infamous for this crime and with no less zeal, contends that he openly teaches diabolical magic in his writings. That Papists trust in amulets and charms after the manner of Gentiles and Jews, Nicolaus Remigius, himself a Papist, admits (Daemonolatria III.3). What shall I say of the wonder-workers and thaumaturges who sought revelations from the Devil? Cornelius à Lapide, in his commentary on 2 Corinthians 11:15, has brought forward the examples of hermits, of the monk Hieronymus and of the monk Valens. Metaphrastes, Caesarius, Cantipratensis, Discipulus, Lipomannus, Surius and others recount many such things here and there. Best known is Petrus Cottonus, a Jesuit, a much-celebrated magician, who from the Devil among several decades of questions asked: "By what text of Scripture can purgatory be proved? What about the honours of my relics? What about the life of the King? What about the preservation of Geneva; what does God want me to know about the plague in Geneva?" Thus Hermolaus Barbarus, Patriarch of Aquileia, according to Giovanni Battista Monlorio, consulted a deceiving demon: "What is Aristotle's entelechy?" If anyone reads attentively the recent writings of the exorcists, such as the monk Michael's account of Louis Gaufridi and of the possessed women, he will not be able to marvel enough at the impiety and stupidity of men who ask the demons to decide controversies of faith, who make them preachers of repentance, who compel them to pour out prayers to God and to perform all the outward duties of religion and piety. I pass over very many such things, which bring infamy upon all Christendom. Meanwhile you see, Redinger, that you would act far more safely in future if you abstained from such slanders and, after your own disgraces, lay hidden with the sons of Scaeva. By pressing too hard on another's nostrils you draw your own blood.

units.la: XIII. Sed nunc ipsos Reformatores nostros intentato crimine exsolvamus. Zwinglius, inquit, narrat, anxiè cogitanti sibi, quomodo verba institutionis Sacramenti corporis Christi exponeret, intempesta 13. Aprilis nocte Spiritum monitorem adfuisse, sed ambigere, utrum ater vel albus fuerit. Crambem millies coctam & recoctam denuo apponere etiamsi sustines, tamen ea nobis mors minimè erit. Primò pessima fidè ais, Zwinglium narrare, sibi spiritum monitorem adfuisse. Atqui ille nec spiritus, nec revelationis meminit, sed monitoris duntaxat. Tu hoc addere de tuo pensi non habuisti, dum lectori mendacio hoc persuadere posses, Zwinglij somnium Diabolicum fuisse. Deinde Zwinglius τὸν δ' εἴνα, a quo per somnium videbatur moneri, nescivit ater an albus esset, hoc est, quis individuo, qualis statu aut conditione, uti paræmia illa Latinis usurpatur, & ab Erasmo in Chiliadibus ex Cicerone, Quintiliano, Catullo & Hieronymo ad Helvidium explicatur. Noli igitur, Redingi, qui in bicipiti Parnasso somniasti, cum illiteratis Monachis putare, album & atrum hic denotare Angelum bonum & Sathanam. Cùm confusæ aut abscuræ ingerunt species rerum aut personarum, aliquando etiam insensatæ, quid mirum, si quis profiteatur se ignorare, quis sit ille, quem per somnium sibi vidisse vel audivisse visus est? Quòd verò Zwinglius evigilans scire aut conjectura assequi, quis Monitor ille fuerit, susque deque habuit, mirari equidem non debes, quia non profitebatur Oneirocriticam, nec cum Oneiromanticis, Inclusis & Monialibus ad somnia & revelationes θεο πέμπτως aspirabat, ne illis accideret, quod Religiosis multis accidisse constat ex Delrione, Cæsario & Aurea Legenda. Habebat Mosen & Prophetas, ut curandum ipsi minimè fuerit, quis Monitor ille esset. Imò ipso hoc inquisitionis neneglectu aperte testatum dederat, se somnio illi minime inhærere, nedum analysin fidei & expositionis controversiæ Eucharisticæ in illud resolvere, sed in solum Dei verbum.
units.tr: XIII. But now let us acquit our Reformers of the charge levelled against them. "Zwingli," he says, "relates that, while he was anxiously thinking how he should expound the words of the institution of the sacrament of Christ's body, on the night of 13 April a monitor Spirit was present to him, but he was uncertain whether it was black or white." Even if you serve up again a cabbage cooked and recooked a thousand times, that will by no means be death to us. First, you say in very bad faith that Zwingli relates that "a monitor Spirit was present to him." Yet he makes no mention of a spirit or of a revelation, but only of a "monitor." You did not think it worth your while to add this from your own resources, since you could persuade the reader by this lie that Zwingli's dream was diabolical. Next, Zwingli says that the one [τὸν δ' εἴνα] by whom he seemed in a dream to be advised "he did not know whether black or white," that is, what individual he was, of what appearance or condition; this proverb is used by Latin writers, and Erasmus in his Adages explains it from Cicero, Quintilian, Catullus and Jerome to Helvidius. So do not, Redinger, who have dreamed on the two-peaked Parnassus, suppose with the unlettered monks that "black and white" here denote the good Angel and Satan. When confused or obscure images of things or persons are presented, sometimes even senseless ones, what wonder if someone professes that he does not know who it was that he seemed to have seen or heard in a dream? But that Zwingli, on waking, cared little whether he could know or conjecture who that monitor was, you ought not to wonder at, because he did not profess the interpretation of dreams, nor did he, like the dream-interpreters, the enclosed women and the nuns, aspire to dreams and revelations sent by God [θεοπέμπτως], lest it happen to him what is known to have happened to many religious, as Delrio, Caesarius and the Golden Legend show. He had Moses and the Prophets, so that it was not at all his concern to know who that monitor was. Indeed, by this very neglect of inquiry he had openly testified that he did not cling to that dream at all, much less resolve the analysis of faith and the exposition of the Eucharistic controversy into it, but into the Word of God alone.

units.la: XIV. Nunc de Calvino. Hunc Epistolâ ad Bucerum monentem, convitijs & maledictis abstineret, respondisse ait: non sui ingenij esse hunc morbum sed genij. Eum ergo genium habuisse familiarem, exterebrare ex verbis hisce conatur. Putavit forte, Calvinum alicubi in Catholica illa Italia, ubi venales reperiri Dæmones vasculis, speculis, phialis, annulis alligatos & inclusos refert Crefpetus, paredrum seu familiarem genium sibi comparâsse. Credo tamen, non ignorâsse Redingium Monachum satis emunctæ naris, quòd genius non spiritum duntaxat familiarem, vel Deum, qui vim obtinet rerum omnium gerendarum, uti loquitur Festus, significet, sed etiam cujusque naturam & cupiditatem carnis, de qua ipsum etiam Apostolum Paulum graviter conquestum legimus septimo ad Romanos. Quem in sensum notæ phrases, genium defraudare, genio indulgere. Quod Græci dicunt Συμόν ἀέξειν, φιλὴ ψυχὴ χαρίζεσθαι. Non erat igitur, cur eam ob phrasin, Cottonianæ societati inaugurari Calvinum satageret. Ita si quis Redingij genium diceret esse hominis sibi nimium placentis, & præ se neminem ferentis, paredri spiritus eidem objecti à nemine sano jure accusari posset.
units.tr: XIV. Now concerning Calvin. He says that when Bucer, in a letter, warned him to abstain from abuse and slander, Calvin replied that this disease was not of his own nature but of his genius. He tries from these words to conclude that Calvin had a familiar genius. He perhaps thought that Calvin had procured for himself a companion or familiar genius somewhere in that Catholic Italy where, according to Crespetus, demons are to be had for sale, shut up and bound in little vessels, mirrors, phials and rings. I believe, however, that Redinger, a monk of fairly sharp nose, was not ignorant that genius signifies not only a familiar spirit, or God "who has power over all things to be done," as Festus puts it, but also a person's nature and carnal desire, of which we read that the Apostle Paul himself gravely complained in Romans 7. To this sense belong the familiar phrases "to defraud one's genius, to indulge one's genius," which the Greeks express as "to feed one's spirit, to gratify one's soul [φιλὴ ψυχὴ χαρίζεσθαι]." There was therefore no reason why Calvin should be eager to be enrolled in the Cottonian fellowship on account of that phrase. So too, if someone said that Redinger's genius was that of a man who is overly pleased with himself and who acknowledges no one above him, no sound man could rightly accuse him of having a familiar spirit.

units.la: XV. Ad Lutherum venimus.
