Eum libro de missa angulari testatum refert adversarius, quòd Diabolum familiari- ter noverit, & plus uno salis modio cum ipso comederit, dulcique alloquio secum conversatus fuerit, imò noctu excitârit se, atque stimulârit, ut contra Missam scriberet, quam in rem ipsi argumenta suppeditaverit. Hanc διάβολον adversarius hausit ex Jesuitæ Serarij de Lutheri Magistro virulento libro, quem pridem obtrivit & solidè retudit Balduinus, ut & Cl. Voetius Desperatæ causæ Papatus pag. 174. &c. ad quos lectorum remitto. Paucis res ita habet. Lutherus suam cum Diabolo de missa privata disputationem literis consignavit, non ut se illo magistro usum ostenderet, cum veritatem jam ante ex verbo Dei didicerit; sed ut suo exemplo probatum daret, quam lubrico Papales illæ rationes fundamento nitantur, & quam non possit omnino illis mens Christiana in tentationibus acquiescere, quas pro stabilienda missa privata in medium afferre solent. Hunc esse narrationis illius scopum, integer contextus docet. Ecquid ergo in Luthero itam ob narrationem damnant? Num colloquium cum Diabolo? Atqui cum eo saepius collocuti sunt Romani Pontifices. Colloquuntur omnium frequentissimi Exorcistæ. Et quod caput est, collocutus est ipse salvator mundi. An quód Lutherus Diabolo mendaci fidem adhibuit? At licet Diabolus sit Pater mendacij, tamen vera quandoque pronuntiat vel invitus, vel inserviens scenæ. Ita Christum vocat Filium Altissimi, Luc.viii.28. Sic tentaturus & ad desperationem adacturus fideles, obijcit illis peccata & peccatorum merita verissima. Eodem modo Lutherum ad desperationem acturus præcipitem, assumpsit id quod erat certissimæ veritatis, videlicet, missam esse idololatricam, adeoque Lutherum tot celebratis privatis missis gravissimi peccati reum esse. Hoc negare Lutherus nec potuit nec debuit. At negavit consequentiam, quam veterator ille struxerat hunc in modum: Qui peccatum gravissimum patravit, ei desperandum. Unde subjungit Lutherus: Non possum negare me peccasse. Sed ibi mentitur Sathan, quod ultra urget ut desperem. Confessus quidem sum coram Diabolo, me peccasse ut Judam, sed converto me ad Christum cum Petro, &c. Num illud damnant, quód Diabolo Missam oppugnanti Lutherus reluctatus non fuerit, cum probabile non sit, idololatriam á Diabolo oppugnari? Atqui Diabolus non tam oppugnabat missam, quam peccatum Lutheri antehac missam celebrantis. Deinde serpens tortuosus cum sit, missam modo oppugnat, modo propugnat. Inservit enim tempori, Ita Delrio ex Surio lib.4. de magia cap.1. q.3. refert, Diabolum aliquando in specie Angelica cuicuidam Abbati apparuisse, eúmque hortatum esse, missam uti celebraret. Atque ita tuam, Redigi, conclusionem, qua viros præstantissimos, quorum eruditioni, gravitati, & morum sanctitati haudquaquam par es, oppugnare non erubuisti, theatricam & merè Poëticam exire intelligis.
units.tr: XV. We come to Luther. His adversary reports that in his book On the Angular Mass Luther testified "that he knew the Devil intimately, and ate more than a peck of salt with him, and conversed with him in sweet discourse; indeed at night he roused and goaded himself, so that he might write against the Mass, for which the Devil supplied him with arguments." This slander the adversary drew from the venomous book of the Jesuit Serarius On Luther's Teacher, which Balduinus long ago wore out and solidly refuted, as did the learned Voetius in Desperata causa Papatus, p. 174 and following, to whom I refer the readers. In brief the matter stands thus. Luther committed to writing his disputation with the Devil about private Mass, not to show that he had been taught by that master, since he had already learned the truth from the Word of God; but to prove by his own example how slippery are those Papal arguments on which they rest, and how a Christian mind cannot at all rest in the temptations which they are wont to bring forward to establish private Mass. The whole context of that narrative shows this to be its purpose. Why then do they condemn Luther on account of that narrative? Is it for the conversation with the Devil? Yet Roman Pontiffs have often conversed with him. The most frequent conversers of all are the exorcists. And, what is the main point, the Saviour of the world himself conversed with him. Or is it because Luther gave credence to the lying Devil? But although the Devil is the father of lies, yet he sometimes speaks the truth, either unwillingly or to serve the stage. Thus he calls Christ "the Son of the Most High" (Luke 8:28). So too, meaning to tempt the faithful and drive them to despair, he sets before them their sins and the most true deserts of their sins. In the same way, meaning to drive Luther headlong into despair, he took up that which was of most certain truth, namely that "the Mass is idolatrous," and so that Luther, by celebrating so many private Masses, was guilty of most grievous sin. Luther could neither deny this nor ought he to have done so. But he denied the inference which that old deceiver had constructed in this manner: "He who has committed the gravest sin ought to despair." Whereupon Luther adds: "I cannot deny that I have sinned. But there Satan lies, when he urges me further to despair. I have indeed confessed before the Devil that I have sinned like Judas, but I turn to Christ with Peter, etc." Do they condemn it that Luther did not resist the Devil when he attacked the Mass? Yet it is not probable that idolatry is attacked by the Devil. Moreover, the Devil was attacking not so much the Mass as Luther's sin in having previously celebrated it. Further, since he is a crafty serpent, he now attacks the Mass and now defends it. For he serves the occasion. Thus Delrio, from Surius (Book 4 On Magic, ch. 1, q. 3), reports that "the Devil at one time appeared in angelic form to a certain abbot and urged him to celebrate Mass." And so, Redinger, you understand that your conclusion, by which you were not ashamed to attack men most eminent, to whose learning, dignity and holiness of life you are in no way equal, is theatrical and purely poetical.

units.la: XVI. Nunc ad vota Monastica. Ea antiquitus frequentata esse, & speciatim à S. Augustino probata, testem allegat Calvinum pag.85.86. Quòd si vel S. Augustinum de moribus Eccl. Cath. cap.31. nec non de Opere Monachorum, vel Calvinum Instit. iv.13. obiter legisset adversarius, reperisset haud dubiè talia, quæ in ruborem ipsum dedissent. Intellexisset nempe, cucullatos hodiernos tum quoad professionem ipsam, tum quoad mores, non minùs differre à veteribus Monachis, quàm simias ab hominibus. Neque adeò sine causa mihi indignatus fuisset Redingius, quòd Monachum ipsum insigniverim. Merito enim ipsum pudere debet hujus professionis & status moderni, cujus nec in S. Scriptura, nec in pia antiquitate vestigium extat. Olim Monastica Collegia seminaria erant ordinis Ecclesiastici. Gregorius Nazianzenus, Basilius, Chrysostomus in monasteriis educati, illinc ad Episcopale munus vocati sunt. Idque suo tempore usitatum fuisse demonstrat Augustinus, ut Ecclesiæ clericos cœnobia ministrarent, uti ex ejus exhortatione facta tum ad Monachos Capraria: Epist.81. tum ad Aurelium Epist.76. liquet. Possidonius Augustini discipulus in Præceptoris vita refert, Augustinum in Monasterio cum doctis habitasse, & dedisse ex suo Collegio Ecclesijs quibusdam rogantibus Episcopos, viros undiquaque doctissimos & piissimos. Erant nempe ipsorum Monasteria non latibula fucorum, sed gymnasia pietatis & virtutis cultorum,uti loquitur Ruffinus lib.2. cap.9. Augustinus de moribus Ecclesiæ cap. 31. & de opere Monachorum, veterem nobis Monachismum repræsentans, inter alia ait, omnem apud eos rigidam exactionem abesse earum rerum, quæ nobis verbo Divino liberæ relinquuntur. At hodierni nihil est, quod severius exigant. Idem AuAugustinus fortiter contendit, non licere Monachis de alieno otiosis vivere. At hodierni praecipuam sanctimoniae partem in otio, mendicitate, infrugiferis & vanissimis speculationibus, quae Christianismo adeo non prosunt, ut obsint magis, collocant. Monachismum Augustinus requirit talem, qui nihil aliud sit quam exercitium adjumentumque ad pietatis & charitatis officia, quae Christianis omnibus commendantur. Hodierni contra in Monachatu meditantur statum perfectionis & meriti. Quinimo pauci homines inter se devincti & conspirantes, ab Ecclesiae sese corpore separant, nullamque adeo charitatis vel unitatis Ecclesiae rationem habent. Veterum Monachorum paupertatem Augustinus praedicat. Hodierni paupertatem mentiti Regales easque certissimas opes possident, quas quibus artibus corrogaverint, nihil attinet dicere. Jam si mores veterum contendere luberet cum moribus modernorum, magis adhuc immanis illa differentia elucesceret. Multa paucis dixit Calvinus Instit. iv. 13:15. nec non Nicolaus a Clemangis nobilis & ipse Papista de corrupto Ecclesiae statu cap. 23. Lubet tamen de eo adscribere Cassandri verba, quae extant Consultat. 25. Quam longe, inquit, Monachatus hodie a prima sui origine degeneraverit, & quantis abusibus contaminatus & deformatus sit, satis per se manifestum est. Nam paulatim religio vera & solida in superstitionem & religionis speciem conversa est, & accrescentibus opibus decrevit pietas, & in ejus locum larvae ceremoniarum successerunt, in quibus verae pietatis operibus paene neglectis summa totius religionis constituta est. quarum ceremoniarum inanis observatio adeo veram apud plerosque Monachos religionem imminuit, ut nusquam fere LICENTIOR ET PROFANIOR vita, quam in nonnullis Monasteriis reperiatur, ita ut mirum non sit, si multorum modio & reprehensioni exponantur. En professi Pontificij, cujus consultationem Theologi Coloniensis laudant in Praefatione anno 1572. edita, de Vobis judicium verissimum!
units.tr: XVI. Now to the monastic vows. He cites Calvin, pp. 85–86, as a witness that these were frequently practised in antiquity and were specifically approved by St Augustine. But if the opponent had read, even in passing, Augustine On the Morals of the Catholic Church chapter 31, and On the Work of Monks, or Calvin, Institutes iv.13, he would undoubtedly have found things that would have put him to shame. He would have understood that the hooded monks of today differ from the ancient monks, both in their profession itself and in their morals, no less than apes differ from men. Nor was Redingius without cause indignant that I branded the monk himself with a mark of disgrace. For he ought to be ashamed of this profession and modern condition, of which no trace exists in Holy Scripture or in pious antiquity. Formerly the monastic colleges were seminaries of the ecclesiastical order. Gregory Nazianzen, Basil, and Chrysostom were educated in monasteries and were called from there to the episcopal office. Augustine shows that this was customary in his own time, that monasteries supplied the clergy of the Church, as is clear from his exhortation to the monks of Capraria, Epistle 81, and to Aurelius, Epistle 76. Possidius, Augustine's disciple, relates in his teacher's life that Augustine lived in the monastery with learned men, and gave from his college to certain churches, when they asked for bishops, men most learned and most pious in every way. Their monasteries were, of course, not hiding-places for drones but gymnasia for the cultivators of piety and virtue, as Rufinus puts it, Book 2, chapter 9. Augustine, in On the Morals of the Church chapter 31 and On the Work of Monks, presenting us with the ancient monasticism, says among other things that among them there was no harsh exaction in those matters which the Divine Word leaves free to us. But the moderns have nothing they exact more strictly. The same Augustine strongly contends that monks may not live in idleness at another's expense. But the moderns place the chief part of holiness in idleness, begging, and unfruitful and most vain speculations, which do not so much benefit Christianity as harm it. Augustine requires a monasticism that is nothing other than an exercise and aid to the duties of piety and charity, which are commended to all Christians. The moderns, on the contrary, in monkhood contemplate a state of perfection and merit. Indeed, a few men bound together and conspiring with one another separate themselves from the body of the Church, and have no regard at all for charity or the unity of the Church. Augustine praises the poverty of the ancient monks. The moderns, pretending poverty, possess royal and very substantial riches, and it is pointless to say by what arts they have amassed them. Now if one wished to set the morals of the ancients against those of the moderns, that huge difference would stand out even more clearly. Calvin said much in a few words, Institutes iv.13.15, and so too Nicolas of Clamanges, a noble Papist himself, on the corrupt state of the Church, chapter 23. Yet it pleases me to add the words of Cassander, found in Consultation 25: How far monkhood has today degenerated from its first origin, and how much it has been contaminated and deformed by great abuses, is clear enough in itself. For gradually true and solid religion has been turned into superstition and a show of religion, and as wealth increased, piety declined, and in its place the masks of ceremonies succeeded, in which, with the works of true piety almost neglected, the whole sum of religion was placed. The empty observance of these ceremonies has so diminished true religion among most monks that nowhere is a life more LICENTIOUS AND PROFANE than in some monasteries, so that it is no wonder if they are exposed to the censure and reproach of many. See, Papists, the most truthful judgment about yourselves, from the work whose Consultation the theologians of Cologne praise in the preface of the edition published in 1572!

units.la: XVII. Orationes & oblationes pro defunctis in Purgatorio laborantibus viguisse quarto quintóve post Christum natum seculo, Redingius pag 87. probare conatur testimonijs Zwinglij in Epicheresi, Bullingeri Decad. 4. Serm. 9. Calvini Instit. III. 5:10. Molinæi Clyp. Fidei pag. 292. Fatentur hi omnes, in veteri Ecclesia orationes pro defunctis obtinuisse. At suscepta eas esse pro defunctis Purgatorianis, nemo eorum profitetur. Imò id ipsum aperte refutat Calvinus Instit. III. 5: 10.
units.tr: XVII. Redingius, p. 87, tries to prove that prayers and offerings for the dead, for souls labouring in Purgatory, flourished in the fourth or fifth century after the birth of Christ, citing the testimonies of Zwingli in Epicheresis, Bullinger, Decad. 4, Sermon 9, Calvin, Institutes III.5.10, and Molinaeus, Clypeus Fidei p. 292. All of these admit that prayers for the dead prevailed in the ancient Church. But that they were offered for the dead in Purgatory, none of them professes. Indeed Calvin, Institutes III.5.10, plainly refutes this very point.

units.la: Neglorientur adversarij nostri, quasi veterem Ecclesiam erroris sui sociam habeant, dico esse longum discrimen. Agebant illi memoriam mortuorum, ne viderentur omnem de ipsis curam abjecisse: sed simul fatebantur se dubitare de ipsorum statu. De Purgatorio certè adeo nihil afferebant, ut pro re incerta haberent. Cæterum si de orationum pro defunctis scopo agatur, distinguendum est totius veteris Ecclesiæ judicium à privatorum in Ecclesia publica Doctorum sententia. Alios illa in orationibus pro defunctis, alios hi fines habuerunt. Ecclesia primitus orationes & oblationes pro defunctis instituit partim ad agendas Deo gratias, eúmque glorificandum in servis suis: partim ad promeritam laudem eorum, qui in Domino obdormissent: partim quò excitarentur alij hoc pacto ad imitationem defunctorum: partim ad fidem, spem, charitatem ordinémque testificandum; fidem quidem, quia vitâ licet functos vivere vitam beatam crederent; spem, quia eódem aspirarent; charitatem, quia dulcem eorum memoriam retinerent; ordinem denique, quia judicarent in Domino mortuos eminentiori forte, infra Christum tamen esse constitutos. Privati verò Doctores quin crediderint, orationes ipsis mortuis esse utiles, nulli inficias imus. Opinio eorum erat, animas ad resurrectionis usque diem in poena damni, in carentia unionis personalis cum corpore, & privatione Divinæ visionis consistente, per preces oblationésque vivorum levari tædio istius moræ, quo resurrectionem plenámque Dei visionem expectarent. Præterea preces addebant, quæ resurrectionem & judicium extremum spectarent. Et citra Purgatorium causas esse potuisse precum pro mortuis, illud argumento est, quod etiam orarint pro Patriarchis, Prophetis, Apostolis, Evangelistis, Martyribus & Confessoribus, quos a morte flammis purgantibus torqueri minime crediderunt ipsi, nec credunt Pontificij. Sed de eo ex Antiquitate Ecclesiastica fuisse differentes adi viros summos, Gerhardum Johannem Vossium Thes. Theolog. pag. 365. 366. &c. nec non Forbesium Instruct. Theol. pag. 689. &c.
units.tr: Let our adversaries not boast, as if they had the ancient Church as an ally in their error. I say there is a great difference. Those men kept the memory of the dead, lest they seem to have cast off all care for them; but at the same time they confessed that they doubted their state. Concerning Purgatory they certainly said so little that they regarded it as an uncertain matter. For the rest, if the aim of prayers for the dead is under discussion, one must distinguish the judgment of the whole ancient Church from the opinion of private teachers in the public Church. Those prayers and offerings had one purpose for the one, and another for the others. The Church first instituted prayers and offerings for the dead partly to give thanks to God and to glorify him in his servants; partly to honour the merited praise of those who had fallen asleep in the Lord; partly so that others might be stirred by this means to imitate the dead; and partly to bear witness to faith, hope, charity, and order: faith, indeed, because they believed that the departed, though no longer living in the body, were living a blessed life; hope, because they aspired to the same; charity, because they retained a sweet memory of them; and order, finally, because they judged that the dead in the Lord were set, though perhaps in a higher place, yet beneath Christ. As for private teachers, we do not at all deny that they believed prayers were useful to the dead themselves. Their opinion was that souls, until the day of resurrection, remain in the pain of loss, in the lack of personal union with the body and the privation of the vision of God, and that through the prayers and offerings of the living they are relieved of the weariness of this delay, with which they await the resurrection and the full vision of God. Moreover, they added prayers that looked to the resurrection and the last judgment. And that there could have been grounds for prayers for the dead apart from Purgatory is shown by the fact that they also prayed for the patriarchs, prophets, apostles, evangelists, martyrs, and confessors, whom they themselves did not believe were tormented by purging flames after death, nor do the Papists believe it. But on this matter, as it stood in ancient ecclesiastical writers, consult the eminent men Gerhard, John Vossius, Thes. Theolog. pp. 365–366, etc., and also Forbes, Instruct. Theol. p. 689, etc.

units.la: XVIII. Sequitur capitalis accusatio adversarij, horrendum isthoc crimen Ecclesijs nostris intentantis, quod earum Doctores veteres Patres, Ecclesiam, Concilia, sanctos, Evangelia, Prophetas, Apostolos, ipsumque Christum ac spiritum S. gravibus errorum censuris notent, pag. 120.
units.tr: XVIII. Next comes the adversary's capital accusation, bringing this horrible charge against our Churches: that they brand with grave censures of error their ancient teachers, the Fathers, the Church, the councils, the saints, the Gospels, the prophets, the apostles, and Christ himself and the Holy Spirit, p. 120.

units.la: En non sibilum serpentis, sed Draconis ungulas! Sed contra feralia haec tela stamus inconniventibus oculis. Non nos illa feriunt, sed levi jactu perfidos in accusatores recidunt, quos harum in Patres, Concilia, Ecclesiam, S. Evangelia Prophetas, Christu & spiritum S. contumeliarum reos nullo negotio peragemus. Nos Patres in rebus fidei uno Deo facimus minores, Illi uni homini profano, Papae, eos subijciunt dedunt; totos nexu & mancupio, cujus nutu instar nummi supputatorij alio atq; alio loco positi, modo tantum significant, modo vix triobolum. Episcopus Bitontinus in Epist. ad Rom. cap. 14, pag. 66. profitetur, se in his quae mysteria fidei tangunt, plus uni summo Pontifici credere, quam mille Augustinis, Hieronymis, Gregorijs. Illi eos invitos trahunt ad patrocinium doctrinae Antichristianae, eos lancinant, adulterant, interpungunt, veru critico, quoties lubet, notant. Indicio esse possunt Indices Expurgatorij, Romanus, Hispanicus, alij, certissimi eorum erga Patres reverentiae testes. Quae patrum, eadem & Conciliorum ratio, quae pro Papae arbitrio vel probant vel improbant. Ecclesia nobis est coetus omnium electorum sub Christi unius regimine fidem minime fucatam profitentium, & vitae sanctitate eandem demonstrantium. Illi eos, qui fidem Christi profitentur, anathematibus perpetuis feriunt, in eos ferro, flamma, rotis saeviunt. Christo Ecclesiae Regi & capiti unico non tam substituerunt quam opposuerunt aliud Ecclesiae caput, seu potius ἀντικείμενον adversarium. Ecclesiae suae cives non faciunt nisi juratos in ejus leges. Clerum, peculium Christi sanguine redemptum, laicorum probrosio nomine detrudunt ad subsellia plorantium, & Ecclesiastico jure & potestate defraudant, omni dominio, addo & nomine cleri ad Hierarchiam, hoc est, Papam, Antistites ab eo inunctos, infulis & litulis insignitos, a quibus Ecclesiam repraesentari asserunt, translato. Tandem Ecclesiam in unum Papam resolventes, reliquis omnibus, sive clerici sint sive Laici, nihil nisi obsequij & sedentariae assentiendi necessitatis gloriam relinquunt. Sanctos, qui vere tales sunt, Patriarchas, Prophetas, B. Virginem, Apostolos aliosque cum Christo regnantes beatos praedicamus in Domino; eorum tanquam ductorum nostrorum, qui sermonem Dei nobis locuti sunt, pie recordamur, exitum conversationis eorum contemplantes; fidem eorum pro virili imitamur; illis denique requiem a laboribus suis toto pectore gratulamur.Illi Sanctos sive vere tales sive δοξαστικῶς in idola commutant, vestientes eos titulis soli Deo competentibus. Fingunt enim omniscios & corda hominum pervidentes, vota ijs faciunt, Templa erigunt, per merita eorum in Canone Missae salutem expetunt, denique nihil non soli Deo competens in eos transferunt. Quod quid aliud est, quam ex ijs per speciem honoris idola facere? B. Virginem quibus contumelijs assiciant, Legendae eorum testantur. Monialis a sacerdote compressae, & postea in lupanar detrusae, vices & personam eam in Monasterio sustinuisse, habet Caesarius de miraculis cap. 35. Alanus de Rupe Monachus jactavit, sibi B. Virginem nupsisse, annulum ei in fidem conjugalem donasse, oscula fixisse, mammas contrectandas & fugendas exhibuisse, referente Balaeo in vita Sixti IV. Eandem solis Hierarchis, hoc est, Missificis, in commissi mysterij executione concedere blasphemat Gabriel Biel lect.4. Sanctos quosdam insigni contumelia praefecerunt porcis, meretricibus &c. Quorundam, veluti Mariæ Ægyptiæ, Macarij, Catharinæ Senensis, Dominici, Francisci &c. vitas sic descripserunt, quasi propositum eis esset, eos differre pipulo, & exsibilandos propinare. Id verò præcipuè indignum & in Sanctos contumeliosum, quòd dum obsoleti quidam & minorum gentium Sancti, qui Papæ eos Cœlo inferenti per auream scalam, canonizationem, rem novam novo nomine insignitam, Sanctitatem suam debent, coluntur Templis, aris, radiato capite ; dum interim ijs sordent Patriarchæ & Prophetæ, quorum in cultu publico nulla mentio, substitutis eorumin locum nescio quarum gentium Diis, Thoma Cantuariensi, Francisco Assisinate, Dominico Calagurritano. Evangelistas & Apostolos utri quæso magis honorant, illîne qui premunt & occultant eorum scripta, an qui ea promunt, & teri volunt manibus Christianorum ? Illi ne, qui Apostolos volunt esse judices de capitibus fidei, an verò illi qui jus hoc ademptum Apostolis transferunt ad Pontificem, qui, si his creditur, potest dispensare contra Apostolum, & condere novos fidei articulos & refigere mandata Dei ? Qui cum Bonaventura Biblia & Psalterium Mariæ ejusmodi concinnant, in quo nomen Jehovæ aut Domini perpetuò mutetur in nomen Dominæ ? Qui probris incessunt scripta Prophetarum & Apostolorum, ea vocantes regulam mutam & imperfectam, nasum cereum, petram scandali, gladium ancipitem, cui fine authoritate Ecclesiæ non plus constet fidei, quàm Alcorano, fabulis Æsopi, Tito Livio ? In Christum ipsum utinam non grandis injuriæ rei essent. Cujus meriti efficaciam illi infringunt, in partem satisfactionis & universæ mediationis ac religiosi honoris vocatis hominibus. Quem quotidie sacrificulorum manibus, quantum in ipsis est, mactant & jugulant. De quo blasphemam vocem effutivit Leo X, quem pro vice-Deo orbis Pontificius salutavit, illas de Christo fabulas multum sibi profuisse. Quem importunum vocavit Thomas, Opusculo 21. cap. 10. quin & mendicum Cardinalis Bellarminus de Monachis cap.45, denique indiscrediscretum Bertrandus in Extravag. Bonif. viii. de Majoritate; & de quo Nicolaus iv. comparans eum cum Franciscο dicit, Christum habuisse quaedam infirma, quibus Franciscus caruerit. Christum enim fugisse & loculos habuisse. Quae duo a Francisco abfuerint; Capite, Exijt de verborum significatione in sexto. De spiritu S. quid dicam? Cujus verbum maledictis impune, uti vidimus, proscindunt; cujus judicium in rebus fidei cavillantur & subterfugiunt; cujus denique testimonium de Divinitate Scripturae non tantum floccipendunt, sed etiam subsannant. Invitus equidem talia purulenta ulcera & carcinomata, caeterequin notissima, detego. Sed cogit adversarij importunitas & maledicentia. Possem addere infinitas injurias & contumelias, quibus summas potestates Clerus Pontificius affecit. Tu igitur, Redingi, qui festucam oculis nostris inhaerere Tibi fingis, non observas trabem, quae tuos penitissime occupat. Disces impositorum domi tuae habitare, & proprium sinum excutere.
units.tr: Behold, not the hiss of a serpent but the claws of a Dragon! Yet we stand against these deadly weapons with unflinching eyes. They do not wound us; with a light throw they fall back upon their treacherous accusers, whom we shall without any trouble convict of these insults against the Fathers, the Councils, the Church, the holy Gospels, the Prophets, Christ and the Holy Spirit. We make the Fathers lesser than the one God in matters of faith. The Papists subject them to one profane man, the Pope. They hand them over entirely in bondage and ownership, and at his nod they are placed now here, now there, like counters on an abacus, sometimes signifying a great deal, sometimes hardly three obols. The Bishop of Bitonto, in Epist. ad Rom. cap. 14, pag. 66., professes that in those matters which touch the mysteries of faith he trusts the one supreme Pontiff more than a thousand Augustines, Jeromes and Gregories. They drag the Fathers, unwilling, into the defence of Antichristian doctrine. They mangle them, corrupt them, punctuate them, and mark them with the critic's obelus whenever they please. The Index Expurgatorius, the Roman, the Spanish and others may serve as evidence, the most certain witnesses of their reverence for the Fathers. The same method applies to the Councils: what the Pope's judgment approves or rejects, that they approve or reject. For us the Church is the assembly of all the elect, who under the rule of the one Christ profess a faith free of pretence and demonstrate it by the holiness of their life. They strike with perpetual anathemas those who profess the faith of Christ, and rage against them with sword, fire and wheel. For Christ, the King and sole Head of the Church, they have not so much substituted as set up another head of the Church, or rather adversary [ἀντικείμενον]. They make citizens of their Church only those sworn to its laws. The clergy, the people Christ redeemed with his blood, they push down with the shameful name of laymen to the benches of the wailing, and defraud them of ecclesiastical right and power; by a transferred use of the name clergy, they assign all dominion and honour to the Hierarchy, that is, to the Pope and the bishops anointed by him and marked with mitres and titles, through whom they claim the Church is represented. Finally, by reducing the Church to the one Pope, they leave to all the others, whether clerics or laymen, nothing but the glory of obedience and of unthinking assent. We proclaim the saints, who are truly such, the Patriarchs, Prophets, the blessed Virgin, the Apostles and the others who reign blessed with Christ, in the Lord. As our guides, who have spoken the word of God to us, we devoutly remember them, contemplating the end of their way of life; we imitate their faith as far as we can; and finally we congratulate them with our whole heart on their rest from their labours. They turn the saints, whether truly such or by opinion [δοξαστικῶς], into idols, clothing them with titles that belong to God alone. For they imagine them all-knowing and seeing into the hearts of men, they make vows to them, raise temples, seek salvation through their merits in the Canon of the Mass, and in short transfer to them everything that belongs to God alone. What else is this than to make idols of them under the appearance of honour? The legends about them testify to the insults with which they treat the blessed Virgin. Caesarius, de miraculis cap. 35, relates that a nun, violated by a priest and afterwards thrust into a brothel, took her place and role in the convent. Alan of Rupe, a monk, boasted that the blessed Virgin had married him, had given him a ring as a pledge of marital faith, had fixed kisses on him and had offered her breasts to be handled and sucked; Balaeus reports this in the life of Sixtus IV. Gabriel Biel, lect.4, blasphemously grants that she is owed to the Hierarchs alone, that is, to the Mass-priests, in the performance of the entrusted mystery. Certain saints they have set over pigs, prostitutes and the like, with notable insult. The lives of some, such as Mary of Egypt, Macarius, Catherine of Siena, Dominic, Francis and others, they have written as if their purpose were to sully them with filth and offer them to be hissed at. This is especially unworthy and insulting to the saints: while certain obscure saints of lesser peoples, who owe their holiness to the Pope bringing them up to heaven by a golden ladder, which is a new thing with a new name, canonization, are worshipped with temples, altars and radiant heads, the Patriarchs and Prophets, of whom there is no mention in public worship, are despised, and in their place are put the gods of I know not what peoples: Thomas of Canterbury, Francis of Assisi, Dominic of Calahorra. Which of the two, I ask, honour the Evangelists and Apostles more: those who press down and hide their writings, or those who bring them forth and want them worn in the hands of Christians? Those who want the Apostles to be judges in the chief matters of faith, or those who transfer this right, taken from the Apostles, to the Pontiff, who, if we believe them, can dispense against the Apostle and frame new articles of faith and undo the commandments of God? Who with Bonaventure compile such a Bible and Psalter for Mary, in which the name Jehovah or Lord is constantly changed into the name Lady? Who assail the writings of the Prophets and Apostles with insults, calling them a dumb and imperfect rule, a waxen nose, a stone of stumbling, a two-edged sword, from which, without the authority of the Church, faith is no more certain than from the Koran, the fables of Aesop or Livy? Would that they were not guilty of great injury against Christ himself! They weaken the efficacy of his merit by summoning men to share in his satisfaction, in the whole of his mediation and in religious honour. Every day, as far as lies in them, they slaughter and butcher him in the hands of little priests. Of him Leo X, whom the Papist world saluted as the vice-God, uttered the blasphemous word that those fables about Christ had greatly profited him. Thomas called him importunate, Opusculo 21. cap. 10.; Cardinal Bellarmine, de Monachis cap. 45, even called him a beggar; finally Bertrand, in Extravag. Bonif. viii., de Majoritate, called him indiscreet. Nicholas IV, comparing him with Francis, says of him: Christ had certain weaknesses which Francis lacked. For Christ fled and had a purse. These two things were absent from Francis; in the chapter Exijt de verborum significatione in the Sixth book. What shall I say of the Holy Spirit? His word they tear to pieces with curses with impunity, as we have seen; his judgment in matters of faith they mock and evade; and finally his testimony to the divinity of Scripture they not only undervalue but even scorn. I reluctantly lay bare such festering ulcers and cancers, which are otherwise very well known. But the impudence and slander of our opponents compel me. I could add countless injuries and insults with which the Papist clergy have assailed the highest powers. You, therefore, Redingus, who pretend that a splinter sticks in our eyes, do not notice the beam that fills your own most deeply. You will learn to dwell among the things imposed upon your house and to shake out your own bosom.

units.la: XIX. Sed nunc propulsanda etiam nobis criminatio, An Calvinus in S. Patres injurius?
units.tr: XIX. But now we must also repel the accusation: Is Calvin unjust toward the Holy Fathers?

units.la: Calvinus hinc inde non erubescere tum Augustinum, tum alios primorum quinque seculorum Patres incusare gravium in materiis fidei errorum, pag. 121. Cujus vero delicti se alligavit Calvinus, si Patres, quos caetera maximo in pretio habuit, verbo Dei non adaequavit, si eos errantes libere redarguit? Etenim hanc ipsi libertatem indulsit S. Hieronymus Apologia contra Jovinianum: De me, ubicunque scripturas non interpretor, sed libere de meo sensu loquor, arguat me Quilibet. Si S. Patres, puta cum Episcopo Bitontino mille Augustinos, Chrysostomos Gregorios unius Papae libidini submisisset, eis Redingij judicio injuriam intulisset nullam. At nunc cum Christo & Apostolis eos subijcit, cum ad immotos Spiritus S. calculos exigit, capital facit, & omnia Deorum hominumque jura inaudito scelere polluit. Sed dixit pro se causam ipse Calvinus in Praefatione ad Regem Galliae. Idem Calvinus, inquis, immodicam censurandi licentiam stringit etiam adversus Concilia Oecumenica. Conciliorum Niceni & Chalcedonensis Patres suis laborâsse infirmitatibus asserit, secutus authoritatem ipsius Leonis Romani Pontificis, qui Concilij Chalcedonensis Patribus ambitionem & inconsultam temeritatem objicere non erubuit. Ad animum sibi revocare debuit adversarius sequentia illa cedro digna Calvini verba, quibus de eo mentem suam explicat: Non aliud intendo, quàm inde colligi posse, spiritum S. sic pias alioquin & sanctas Synodos gubernâsse, ut interim aliquid humanitus eis accidere sineret, ne nimium hominibus consideremus.
units.tr: Calvin, here and there, is not ashamed to accuse both Augustine and other Fathers of the first five centuries of grave errors in matters of faith, p. 121. But what offence has Calvin bound himself to, if he did not put the Fathers, whom he otherwise held in the highest esteem, on a level with the Word of God, and if he freely refuted them when they erred? Indeed, St. Jerome granted himself this same freedom in his Apology against Jovinian: Concerning me, wherever I do not interpret the Scriptures but speak freely from my own opinion, let anyone at all refute me. If Calvin had subjected the Holy Fathers, say with the Bishop of Bitonto, a thousand Augustines, Chrysostoms and Gregorys, to the lust of a single Pope, he would have done no injury to them by Redingius' judgment. But now, when he places them alongside Christ and the Apostles, when he brings them to the unerring judgment of the Holy Spirit, he makes them capital, and pollutes all the laws of God and men with an unheard-of crime. Yet Calvin himself pleaded his case in his Preface to the King of France. The same Calvin, you say, restrains an excessive license of censure even against the Ecumenical Councils. He asserts that the Fathers of the Councils of Nicaea and Chalcedon laboured under their own weaknesses, following the authority of Leo, the Roman Pontiff himself, who did not hesitate to charge the Fathers of the Council of Chalcedon with ambition and rash lack of counsel. Your opponent ought to have recalled to mind those words of Calvin, worthy of cedar, in which he explains his own mind on this point: I intend nothing other than that it may be gathered from this that the Spirit of God so governed otherwise holy and pious synods that he nonetheless allowed something human to befall them, lest we should think too much of men.

units.la: X X. Sed pergis, & Zwinglio nigrum theta praefigis, quód in Epicherefi sua scribere non erubuerit: Apostolos ex indulgentia permisisse quibusdam infirmis pro mortuis orare, sed Chrysostomus tamen & Augustinus vere tradiderint, huncce morem ab Apostolis usque ad se manâsse. Taedet puerilium nugarum, quibus hic homo sibi supra modum suffenus conficere se posse sperávit, ut Reformatores nostri blasphemiarum rei crederentur. Negat Zwinglius, induci se posse, ut credat, morem orandi pro defunctis Apostolos authores habere. Ponit tamen, non concedit, morem eum ab Apostolis processisse, eorum erga infirmos indulgentiae & συγγνωμην tribui posse putat. Atque sic hodieque faciendum arbitratur, si qui adeo tenui fide sunt, ut fideles parentes caelesti Domino anxijs precibus commendare cupiant, eos importune abijciendos non esse, quia Christus linum fumigans non extinxit, & ὀλιγοπίστας discipulos toleravit. Sed in infirmitate permanere, & quod quidam lucriones faciunt, stabilire, id vero, inquit ille, nullis permittere debemus. Quid hic in Zwinglio desiderare potes, Redingi? An hoc est Apostolos gravibus errorum censuris perstringere? An ergo qui asserit, Deum tolerâsse pravos Judaeorum mores, polygamiam & divortia; Mosen perfidis maritis divortij quendam ordinem praescripsisse; Christum discipulos de regno Deierrantes non abjecisse; Apostolum permisisse ut circumcideretur Timotheus; iccicro Deum, Christum, MoMosen, Apostolum gravibus errorum censuris calumniosè notat? Tam stolidæ argumentationes indicium præbent, Vos à bona & mente & causa desertos, & ad incitas jam pridem redactos esse.
units.tr: XX. But you go on, and you brand Zwingli with a black theta, because in his Epicheirema he was not ashamed to write: The Apostles allowed some weak people, out of indulgence, to pray for the dead, but Chrysostom and Augustine truly relate that this custom flowed down from the Apostles to their own time. I am weary of the childish trifles by which this man hoped, beyond measure pleased with himself, to make our Reformers appear guilty of blasphemy. Zwingli denies that anyone can be brought to believe that the Apostles were the authors of the custom of praying for the dead. Yet he states, without conceding, that the custom did come from the Apostles, and he thinks it can be attributed to their indulgence and indulgence [συγγνώμην] toward the weak. And so he thinks it should be done even today: if some are so slight in faith that they wish to commend their believing parents to the heavenly Lord with anxious prayers, they should not be rudely cast off, since Christ did not quench the smoking flax and tolerated his disciples of little faith [ὀλιγοπίστας]. But to persist in weakness, and, as some profiteers do, to make it permanent, this, he says, we must permit to nobody. What can you find to desire in Zwingli here, Redingius? Is this to lash the Apostles with grave censures of error? So, then, does he who asserts that God tolerated the wicked customs of the Jews, polygamy and divorces; that Moses prescribed a certain form of divorce for faithless husbands; that Christ did not cast off his disciples who erred about the kingdom of God; that the Apostle allowed Timothy to be circumcised, slander God, Christ, Moses and the Apostle with grave censures of error? Such foolish arguments show that you have been deserted by both sound mind and sound cause, and have long since been reduced to tilting at windmills.

units.la: XXI. Qua verò fronte Johannem Evangelistam idololatriæ insimulatum à Calvino & Molinæo scribere audes? Calvinus equidem narrat, accidisse Johanni, ut prosterneretur coram Angelo, in quo Divini Numinis refulgebat fulgor, cui tamen responsum sit statim: Vide ne feceris, conservus tuus sum, Deum adora. Numquid falsò hoc narravit? An ex narratione ea sequitur, idololatriæ accusatum esse à Calvino Johannem? Id si verum est, in ipsam Scripturam, quæ authenticè hoc narravit, accusationis hujus culpa redundabit. Molinæus non idololatriæ accusat Johannem, sed ex responso Angeli, tralatitiam duliæ & latriæ distinctionem oppugnat. Si enim ea distinctio Angelo innotuisset, non opus fuisset, ut in universum adorationem abnueret, sed duleuticam quidem admisisset, at latreuticam solam respuisset.
units.tr: XXI. With what face do you dare to write that John the Evangelist was accused of idolatry by Calvin and Molinaeus? Calvin indeed relates that it happened to John that he fell prostrate before an Angel, in whom the splendour of the divine majesty shone, to whom nevertheless an answer was immediately given: See that you do not; I am your fellow servant; worship God. Did he relate this falsely? Or does it follow from that narrative that John was accused of idolatry by Calvin? If that is true, the blame of this accusation will fall back upon Scripture itself, which related this authentically. Molinaeus does not accuse John of idolatry, but from the Angel's answer he attacks the traditional distinction between dulia and latria. For if that distinction had been known to the Angel, there would have been no need for him to refuse adoration altogether; he would have admitted the duleutic kind but rejected the latreutic kind alone.

units.la: XXII. Instas hunc in modum: Idem Calvini spiritus adversus ipsum Spiritum S. se attollit Inst. 1.8:1. & III.6:1. afferendo, Spiritum Dei non exactè nec perpetuò methodicam rationem in S. literis observâsse: interdum verò rudi, crasso & barbaro stylo usum esse. Os hominis, insignémque impudentiam cognoscite! Calvinus utrobique Scripturarum Divinitatem probat ex simplicitate styli, sine ulla affectatione & ostentatione docentis. Ostendit, non sine eximia Dei providentia factum, ut sublimia Regni cœlestis mysteria sub contemptibili verborum humilitate bona ex parte traderentur, ne si splendidiore eloquentia illustrata forent, cavillarentur impij, solam ejus vim hic regnare. Nunc verò, inquit, cúm inculta illa & tantúm non rudis simplicitas majorem sui reverentiam excitet, quám ulla Rhetorum facundia, quid judicare licet nisi potentiorem Scripturæ S. vim veritatis constare, quàm ut verborum arte indigeat? Simplicitatem vocat incultam & tantùm non rudem. Barbaram & crassam non vocat, sed id barbarè & crassè mentitur adversarius, majorem ut invidiam conflaret Calvino. Quòd verò incultam & tantùm non rudem simplicitatem vocat, in eo nec à Scriptura ipsa, nec à veteris Ecclesiæ sensu recessit. Paulus 2.Cor.x1.6. non negat se esse ἰδιώτην λόγῳ, idiotam sermone. Et 1.Cor.1:17. fatetur, se Evangelium prædicare non in sapientia sermonis, ne evacuetur crux Christi. Confer. 1.Cor.2:1.4:13. ubi suam prædicationem non persuasoriis humanæ sapientiæ verbis, sed ostensione Spiritûs & sapientiæ commendabilem esse ait. Patres dictionem Apostolorum vocârunt non simpliciter rudem & incultam, sed ἀγεωμετρικῶς, σολοικίζοντας, βαρβαρίζοντας, ἰδιωτικὴν, uti docet magnus Salmasius Hellenisticæ pag.260. &c. Et rationem reddit Isidorus Pelusiota satis idoneam, quia hominibus naturæ infimæ & imbecillæ leges ferebant, qui humanis opus habebant verbis. Iccirco, inquit, ἰδιωτικαῖς λέξεσιν ἐκέρασε τὰ θεῖα κηρύγματα, idioticis seu incultis locutionibus doctrinam cælestem temperavit. Arnobius adversus Gentes lib.1. pag.m.35. Trivialis & sordidus sermo est. Nunquam enim veritas sectata est fucum, nec quod exploratum & certum est, circumduci se patitur orationis per ambitum langiorem. An igitur scriptores sacros, qui de se hoc fassi sunt, nec non Ecclesiasticos Calvino hic longè crudiores eâdem notâ inuret Redingius, quòd se attollant supra Spiritum Dei? Meminerit tamen adversarius, Calvinum incultam & tantùm non rudem simplicitatem opponere Rhetorum mangoniis, & mellitis, ut illi loqui amant, verborum globulis. Neque enim is inficiatur, quin suam Sacri Scriptores, Rhetoricam, quam toties non immeritò ipsi etiam Patres commendant, sed non sucatam illam & ad humani ingenij leges exactam, adhibuerint.
units.tr: XXII. You press the point in this way: The same spirit of Calvin raises itself against the Holy Spirit himself, Inst. 1.8:1 and III.6:1, asserting that the Spirit of God did not observe a precise and continuous methodical order in the Holy Scriptures, and that at times he used a rude, coarse and barbarous style. Behold the mouth and the remarkable impudence of the man! Calvin in both places proves the divinity of the Scriptures from the simplicity of their style, without any affectation or display in the teacher. He shows that it was not without a remarkable providence of God that the lofty mysteries of the heavenly kingdom were for the most part delivered under the contemptible humility of words, lest, if they were illuminated by more splendid eloquence, the impious would cavil, and would suppose that only their force reigned here. But now, he says, since that uncultivated and almost rude simplicity arouses greater reverence for itself than any eloquence of the Rhetoricians, what can we judge except that the power of the Holy Scripture's truth is too strong to need the art of words? He calls the simplicity uncultivated and almost rude. He does not call it barbarous and coarse; your opponent lies in this, saying it barbarously and coarsely, so as to stir up greater hatred against Calvin. But in calling it uncultivated and almost rude simplicity, he departed neither from Scripture itself nor from the sense of the ancient Church. Paul, 2 Cor. 11:6, does not deny that he is ἰδιώτην λόγῳ, an amateur in speech [idiotam sermone]. And at 1 Cor. 1:17 he confesses that he preaches the Gospel not in wisdom of speech, lest the cross of Christ be emptied. Compare 1 Cor. 2:1, 4:13, where he says that his preaching is commendable not by the persuasive words of human wisdom but by the demonstration of the Spirit and of power. The Fathers called the diction of the Apostles not simply rude and uncultivated, but ungeometrical, solecistic, barbarizing, idiotic [ἀγεωμετρικῶς, σολοικίζοντας, βαρβαρίζοντας, ἰδιωτικὴν], as the great Salmasius teaches in his Hellenistica, p. 260, etc. And Isidore of Pelusium gives a reason that is quite sound: the laws were given to men of the lowest and weakest nature, who had need of human words. For this reason, he says, he mingled the divine proclamations with idiotic, that is, uncultivated, expressions [ἰδιωτικαῖς λέξεσιν ἐκέρασε τὰ θεῖα κηρύγματα]. Arnobius, Against the Gentiles, book 1, p. 35: Their speech is trivial and mean. For truth never sought ornament, nor does what is known and certain allow itself to be led round by a long circuit of words. Will Redingius then brand with the same mark the sacred writers, who confessed this about themselves, and the ecclesiastical writers, far ruder than Calvin here, for raising themselves above the Spirit of God? Yet let your opponent remember that Calvin sets an uncultivated and almost rude simplicity against the rhetorician's ornaments and honeyed balls of words, as they love to call them. For he does not deny that the sacred writers employed their own Rhetoric, which the Fathers themselves so often and not without reason commend, but not that sugared kind, shaped to the laws of human talent.

units.la: XXIII. Quæ de VVollebio & Szegedino garris, ex eo- dem ineptiendi genio proficiscuntur.
units.tr: XXIII. What Wollebius and Szegedinus babble comes from the same silly temperament.

units.la: Usum azymi in Cœna Domini vocant profanationem ac Judaicam superstitionem. Ergo etiam Christum in Cœnæ institutione azymo usum profana-
units.tr: They call the use of unleavened bread at the Lord's Supper a profanation and Jewish superstition. So you infer that Christ too, in instituting the Supper with unleavened bread, is charged with profana-

units.la: Wollebius & Szegedinus vindicantur. fanationis, & superstitionis Judaicæ insimulari colligis. Atqui illi loquuntur de usu azymi inter Christianos cum necessitatis opinione conjuncto. Quomodo merito vos profanationis hujus & superstitionis Judaicæ reos peragimus, qui eandem necessitatem usus azymi fingitis, & secus sentientibus eo nomine convitium facitis. At Christus in prima coena etsi ex accidente temporis non alio quam azymo uti potuit, legem tamen necessitatis imposterum non indixit.
units.tr: Wollebius and Szegedinus are vindicated. tion and Jewish superstition. But they are speaking of the use of unleavened bread among Christians joined to the belief that it is necessary. How rightly we accuse you of this profanation and Jewish superstition, when you feign this same necessity for the use of unleavened bread and heap abuse on those who think otherwise! But Christ, at the first Supper, although by the circumstance of the time he could use nothing but unleavened bread, did not lay down a law of necessity for the future.

units.la: XXIV. Sic dirissimæ accusationis tela infracta sunt. Gradum nunc promovemus ad id, quod arx & propugnaculum est totius Papatus, primatum nimirum Petri & Papæ Romani. Hunc veteribus agnitum esse, testes allegantur Reformati Doctores, speciatim Bullingerus Decad. 5. Serm. 2. SS. Turpiter, Calvinus Instit. iv. 6:6. & 7:5. quos nolentes volentes fateri debuisse ait antagonista, tum quod veteres Ecclesiæ scriptores sint testificati de primatu Petri: tum quod verba illa; Et super hanc petram ædificabo Ecclesiam; ex sensu Patrum tum Græcorum tum Latinorum accipienda sint de Petro: tum denique, quod nullum fuerit tempus, quo non Romana sedes imperium in alias Ecclesias (ex ipso scilicet, uti S. Patres probant, jure Divino) appetiverit pag. 179. Quin & Papam esse successorem Petri, fatentes introducit Alstedium Chronol. cap. 24. & Calvinum Instit. iv. 7:5. pag. 181. Primatum ordinis & honoris, πρεσβεῖαν præsidentiam, uti Græci vocant Patres, B. Petro nullis ingratis nostris detulerunt nonnulli. Hoc fatentur nostri. Primatum vero imperij & jurisdictionis, ἐξουσίας καὶ ἀυθεντίας, seu potius, uti Salmasius vocavit, Suprematum, & Papalem illam omnipotentiam tribuit nemo. Verba Christi: Super hanc petram ædificabo Ecclesiam meam, nonnullos Patres de Petro exposuisse largitur Calvinus. Sed ij ipsi à Papistarum sententia sunt alienissimi. Agnoscunt Petrum esse appellatum Petram, sive ratione fidei & confessionis, sive τὴν τιμὴν ὀνόματι potius, quàm τὴν φύσιν πεσγματι. Aliàs propria & essentialia Petræ prædicata soli Deo competere, nulli diffitentur. Quoad Episcopos Romanos, fatetur Calvinus, nullum tempus fuisse, quo non Romana sedes in alias imperium appetiverit. Appetijsse scribit. At jure Divino sibi debitum imperium appetijsse, non Calvini assertio est, sed glossa Redingij. Qui si Mysterium iniquitatis illustris Mornæi Plessiaci legisset, appetitum sane & ambitum à Pontificibus imperium, at diu ab Ecclesia negatum, & sero admodum, invalescente eorundem dominatione, cordatis tamen nunquam non reclamantibus, exambitum intellexisset. De Papæ in locum Petri successione ne gry quidem l. c. habet Calvinus. Alstedius Petrum Romam venisse concedit. Negat tamen, ibi 2 5 annos consedisse; & disceptationem ipsum inter & Simonem magum Θεαμαγικὴν potius quàm ἰσοεικὴν fuisse asserit. Patres pro dignitate R. Episcopi, argumento à successione petito usos esse, satis constat. Sed intellexerunt cum locali & personali successione in urbe Romana & Episcopatu ejus celeberrimo, conjunctam perpetuam ejusdem doctrinæ & fidei, quasi per manus sibi succedentium Episcoporum traditionem. Hoc facere licuit Irenæo & Tertulliano contra hæreticos, Optato & Augustino contra Manichæos & Donatistas. Erant enim secula illa doctrinæ Apostolicæ tenacia, & aureis similima. Saltem tam notoria doctrinæ mutatio apud primos illos Romanos Episcopos, quanta in hodiernis Pontificibus non apparuit. Cæterum quam successionem intellexerint, prodidit ipse Irenæus lib. 111.43. ubi cum Episcopatus successione conjungit charisma veritatis secundum placitum Patris. Et Ambrosius de Pœnit. lib. 1.6. inquit : Non habet Petri hæreditatem, qui Petri non habet fidem. Dent igitur operam Romani Pontifices, ut Petri fidem postliminio in ptæcordia admittant. Sic de hæreditate ejus controversiam ipsis non movebimus.
units.tr: XXIV. In this way the darts of this most dreadful accusation are blunted. Now we advance to what is the citadel and bulwark of the whole Papacy, namely the primacy of Peter and of the Roman Pope. The Reformed teachers are cited as witnesses that the ancients acknowledged this, especially Bullinger, Decad. 5, Serm. 2, and Calvin, Institutes iv. 6:6 and 7:5, whom the opponent says he must, willing or unwilling, admit: first, that the ancient writers of the Church bore witness to the primacy of Peter; second, that those words, "And upon this rock I will build the Church," must be understood of Peter according to the sense of the Fathers, both Greek and Latin; and finally, that there has never been a time when the Roman see did not seek empire over the other Churches (by divine right, namely, as the holy Fathers prove) p. 179. Indeed he also brings in Alsted, Chronology ch. 24, and Calvin, Institutes iv. 7:5, p. 181, confessing that the Pope is the successor of Peter. Some have granted to the blessed Peter the primacy of order and honour, the presidency (which the Greek Fathers call presbeia), and none of our people deny it. Our people admit this. But the primacy of power and jurisdiction, [exousias kai authentias], or rather, as Salmasius called it, the supremacy, and that Papal omnipotence, no one grants. That some Fathers expounded the words of Christ, "Upon this rock I will build my Church," of Peter, Calvin concedes; but those very men are most remote from the Papists' opinion. They acknowledge that Peter was called a rock either by reason of his faith and confession, or rather in name by honour, [tēn timēn onomati], not in nature [tēn physin pragmati]. No one denies that the proper and essential predicates of a rock belong to God alone. As for the Roman bishops, Calvin admits that there has never been a time when the Roman see did not seek empire over others. He writes that it sought it. But that it sought an empire due to it by divine right is not Calvin's assertion but Redingius' gloss. If Redingius had read the famous Mystery of Iniquity of Mornay du Plessis, he would have understood that the empire was indeed sought and ambitiously pursued by the Pontiffs, yet long denied by the Church, and very late admitted, when their domination was growing strong, though sensible men had always objected, and it was an ambitious usurpation. Calvin, in the passage cited, says nothing at all about the succession of the Pope to the place of Peter. Alsted concedes that Peter came to Rome. He denies, however, that he sat there twenty-five years, and he asserts that the contest between Peter and Simon Magus was a spectacle contest [theamatikēn] rather than a contest of proofs [isodynamikēn]. It is quite clear that the Fathers, out of regard for the dignity of the Roman bishop, used the argument drawn from succession. But they understood it as a perpetual succession of the same doctrine and faith, joined with the local and personal succession in the city of Rome and its most famous episcopate, as though handed down through the hands of the bishops succeeding one another. Irenaeus and Tertullian could do this against the heretics, and Optatus and Augustine against the Manichaeans and Donatists. For those ages were tenacious of apostolic doctrine and very like the golden age. At least, no change in doctrine so notorious as appears among the Popes of today appeared among those first Roman bishops. Moreover, what succession they understood, Irenaeus himself has declared, Book 3, ch. 4 (or 3), where he joins with the succession of bishops the charism of truth according to the good pleasure of the Father. And Ambrose, On Repentance, Book 1, ch. 6, says: He does not have the inheritance of Peter who does not have the faith of Peter. Let the Roman Pontiffs therefore take care to admit the faith of Peter back into their hearts by right of return. Thus we shall not raise a controversy with them about his inheritance.

units.la: XXV. Innatum fingendi cacoethes prodit adversarius
units.tr: XXV. The innate itch for fabrication betrays the opponent.

units.la: pag 179. ubi Calvinum Institit. iv. 10. fateri scribit, quod opinio de septem Sacramentis in Ecclesia radices egerit primis quinque seculis a tempore Apostolorum. Quæ enim confecutio est: Calvinus ait, opinionem de septem Sacramentis vetustate radices egisse. Ergo fatetur, primis quinque seculis eam in Ecclesia radices egisse. An nulla alia vetustas est, quàm primorumquinque seculorum? Vetustatem intellexit Calvinus, sed Lombardo & Concilio Florentino non anteriorem. Fraudem hominis non melius detexerimus, quàm repraesentatis ipsius Calvini verbis disertissimis, quae ita habent: Si veteris Ecclesiae authoritate premere nos velint, dico eos fumum facere. Nunquam enim apud Ecclesiasticos Scriptores numerus hic septenarius invenitur: nec satis constat, quo primùm tempore obrepserit. Fateor quidem, in vocabulo Sacramenti esse interdum liberiores. Sed quid eo significabant? Nempe ceremonias omnes & externos ritus, omniaque pietatis exercitia. Cùm autem de signis loquuntur, quae Divinae in nos gratiae esse testimonia debent, duobus istis, Baptismo & Eucharistia contenti sunt. Quid verbis his expressius? Si veri nominis Sacramenta forent, quotquot apud Patres, & in vulgata versione juxta Concilij Tridentini definitionem authentica, exotico hoc Sacramenti nomine veniunt, vix septuagenarius numerus sufficeret. Augustino Epistola 5. omne signum est Sacramentum. Hilario in Mathaeum can. 11.12.13. Sacramenti nomine veniunt oratio, lachrymae, Scriptura, fames, sitis: Bernhardo lotio pedum. In vulgata versione Apoc. xvii.7. meretrix Babylonica & Bestia Apoc. Sacramenti notione veniunt. An igitur etiam meretrix Babylonica & Bestia Apocalyptica huncce Sacramentorum apud vos numerum augebunt? En quò te tua de nomine Sacramenti argutatio transversum abriperet!
units.tr: p. 179, where he writes that Calvin, Institutes iv. 10, confesses that the opinion about seven Sacraments took root in the Church within the first five centuries from the time of the Apostles. What is the inference? "Calvin says the opinion about seven Sacraments took root through antiquity. Therefore he confesses that it took root in the Church within the first five centuries." Is there no other antiquity than that of the first five centuries? Calvin understood antiquity, but one not earlier than Lombard and the Council of Florence. We could not expose the man's fraud better than by setting before him the very clear words of Calvin himself, which read thus: If they wish to press us with the authority of the ancient Church, I say they make smoke. For this septenary number is never found among ecclesiastical writers, nor is it sufficiently clear at what time it first crept in. I admit indeed that in the word sacrament they are sometimes freer. But what did they mean by it? Namely all ceremonies and external rites, and all the exercises of piety. When, however, they speak of signs, which ought to be testimonies of divine grace toward us, they are content with those two, Baptism and the Eucharist. What could be more explicit than these words? If those things that, among the Fathers and in the Vulgate version, are authentically (according to the definition of the Council of Trent) called by this exotic name of sacrament were real sacraments, scarcely a number of seventy would suffice. In Augustine, Epistle 5: every sign is a sacrament. In Hilary on Matthew, canons 11, 12, 13, the name of sacrament is given to prayer, tears, Scripture, hunger, thirst; in Bernard, the washing of feet. In the Vulgate version, Rev. 17:7, the Babylonian harlot and the Beast of the Apocalypse are called by the notion of sacrament. Will the Babylonian harlot and the Apocalyptic Beast then also increase this number of Sacraments among you? See where your quibbling about the word "sacrament" would drag you across the grain!

units.la: XXVI. Calvinum & Luherum incessere pergis. Et il-
units.tr: XXVI. You persist in assailing Calvin and Luther. As for the first of them,

units.la: lum quidem, quòd ad fidem & authoritatem ex falso miraculo sibi conciliandam, eum qui se mortuum fingebat, simulate resuscitare volens, ex vivis ad inferos transmiserit. Lutherum verò, quòd daemoniacum aggressus, turpi & obscoena sugâ sibi salutem quaerere coactus fuerit, pag. 188.189. Historiae utriusque testes quaeso cur nullos ibi allegas? Ratio nobis subo-let. Iet. Non alios allegare poteras, quàm de Luthero Staphylum & Cochleum ; de Calvino Laurentium Surium Carthusianum & Bolsecum. Sic non immeritò verebàre, ne tibi occentaremus fabulam accusatæ á cane ovis. Deposcebat ille in judicio debitum ab ove, cujus debendi hæc rea non erat. Jussus canis producere testes,allegabat tres, lupum, milvum & accipitrem. Sic tu convicturus eras Calvinum testimonio Surij & Bolsceci ; Lutherum verò Staphyli & Cochlei. Qui verò illi ? Lupus,milvus, accipiter. Hostes aperti, calumniatores insignes, duo apostatæ, intestabiles omnes. Scilicet illis fidem habebimus, cùm constet nobis, Calvinum in Præfatione institutionum ; Lutherum verò Domin. 2. Advent. in Explic. Epist. homines á miraculis revocâffe ad doctrinam. Quod de ijs fatetur etiam Maldonatus Jesuita Comment. in Joh. cap.2. Surius infelix ille & insulsus Historicus, quem probi historici neullum quidem numerum implêffe nullo negotio probare possem, unde fidem facit huic de Calvino mendacio ? Hæc quidem, inquit ad A.1538. de illo Calvino multáque alia sparsit fama. Egregié & ἀνεξιβῶς. Ita soliti scilicet Livius, Herodianus, Thuanus, Sleidanus. Atqui vel pueri nôrunt, fama cujusmodi malum fit, nempe tam sicti pravique tenax, quàm nesciarecti. Ait ille Cretenfis, persuasisse Calvinum misero cuidam, ut se pateretur tanquam mortuum in Templum deportari. Nondum sciverat Carthusianus ille κατα,βιῶσας Coloniæ, Genevenses eo tempore lege & consuetudine publica mortuos suos extra Templum sepelivisse. Id enim fi fcivitfet, mentitus esset fi non castius saltem cautiùs. Tum mirari subit, cùm Genevæ & in vicinia Calvinus habuerit æmulos & juratos hostes, qui tamen ipsi viventi nihil tale impegerunt unquam, quâ tandem rimâ totum hoc manaverit & penetra verit ad Arcadiam illam Carthufianam ? Sed ejusmodi putida mendacia post mortem virorum Sanctorum sparsa non est cur adeò miremur, cùm non puduerit Papistas, talia de vivis spargere. Fabulam de Lutheri & Calvini ignominiosa morte ipsi viventes audiverunt, quam ille quidem scripto publico confutavit. Bezam in agone mortis Romanam ad Ecclesiam aspirâsse, audiebat etiam ipse & refellebat vivus.
units.tr: That Calvin, because, to win faith and authority for himself by a false miracle, he wished to feign the resurrection of a man who pretended to be dead, and so sent him from the living to the dead, and that Luther, because, having attacked a demoniac, he was forced to seek his safety in a shameful and obscene flight, p. 188–189. I ask you, witnesses of both histories, why do you cite none here? The reason is not hard to guess. You could cite no one except Staphylus and Cochlaeus against Luther, and against Calvin Laurentius Surius the Carthusian and Bolsec. So we rightly fear that we are being sung the fable of the sheep accused by the dog. The dog demanded in court a debt from the sheep, which she did not owe. Ordered to produce witnesses, the dog named three: the wolf, the kite and the hawk. So you were going to convict Calvin by the testimony of Surius and Bolsec, and Luther by that of Staphylus and Cochlaeus. But who are they? A wolf, a kite, a hawk: open enemies, notorious slanderers, two apostates, all of them unworthy of belief. Of course we shall put our faith in them, when we know that Calvin, in the Preface to the Institutes, and Luther, in the Second Sunday of Advent in his Explication of the Epistle, declared that men had been called back from miracles to doctrine. Maldonatus the Jesuit also admits this of them in his commentary on John chapter 2. That wretched and silly historian Surius, whom I could easily prove never fulfilled a single rule of honest historians, on what ground does he win credence for this lie about Calvin? These things indeed, he says, at the year 1538, and much else, rumour has spread about that Calvin. Admirably, and without examination [ἀνεξιβῶς]. Livy, Herodian, Thuanus and Sleidan, of course, are in the habit of doing the same. Yet even boys know what a bad thing rumour is: as tenacious of the false and wicked as ignorant of the true. That Cretan says that Calvin persuaded a wretched man to let himself be carried into the church as if dead. That Carthusian had not yet learned that the Genevans at that time, by public law and custom, buried their dead outside the church. Had he known it, he would have lied less shamelessly, if not more cautiously. Then one wonders: since Calvin had rivals and sworn enemies in Geneva and its neighbourhood, who nevertheless never charged him with anything of the kind while he was alive, by what crack did this whole story seep out and penetrate into that Carthusian Arcadia [καταβιώσας] at Cologne? But we need not be so surprised that such foul lies were spread after the death of holy men, since the Papists were not ashamed to spread such things about the living. The fable of the ignominious death of Luther and Calvin was heard by them while still alive, and Calvin refuted it in a public writing. That Beza, in his death agony, turned towards the Roman Church, he too heard and refuted while still alive.

units.la: XXVII. Quód si nunc miracula, quæ Pontificij, Monachi inprimis, frontem perfricantes, & spiritu mendacij afflati, non finxerunt tantùm, sed etiam ficta theatronicè jactârunt, & adhucdum jactant, prodere animum inducerem, equidem mecharte deficerent.
units.tr: XXVII. If I were now to resolve to disclose the miracles which the Papists, especially the monks, have not only invented with brazen faces and under the inspiration of the spirit of lies, but also theatrically boasted of and still boast of, my paper would indeed run out.

units.la: Non possum tamen, quin speciminis loco, duo eáque recentissima ψόδ' ας τέφατα prodigiosa menda-cia, totidem miracula nimirum, quæ in stabilimentum doctrinæ Pontificiæ in hac ipsa civitate Tigurina, dilecta patria nostra, patrata esse, Coloniæ publicis Jesuitarum novellis non ita pridem impudentissimè vulgatum est. Ac quod prius attinet, anni effluxerunt quinque, ex quo novellæ Latinæ Coloniæ authoribus Jesuitis impressæ, & vulgatæ ferebant, Tigurum venisse Catholicum quendam, (Pontificium puta) qui repentino ibi morbo correptus jusserit Catholicum sacerdotem accersiri, apud quem animæ noxas deponeret, & ab eodem viatico ad extremum iter instrueretur. Ægri petitione ad rabulam Acatholicum, (qui antea orthodoxus fuerat) delata, adornatam Comœdiam mox in tragœdiam desituram. Admissum ad ægrum audivisse confitentem, ritúque simulato Romano absolvisse: subinde sacrum viaticum jussum porrigere, prompsisse frustillum rapi, jamque fuisse in eo, ut & sic ægro illuderet, cùm sic pulsatas fores cubiculi, jussum expectare foris, qui pulsare audiebatur, dum scena absolveretur. At illum fortius institisse iterato pulsatu, quem cùm tertiò repetijsset, non expectatâ ingrediendi licentiâ, reclusisse januam, & præconem nihil minus cogitantem, unâ cum frusto suo rapuisse, nullo ejusdem relicto vestigio. Desiderari miserum etiamnum, & absentiâ suâ manifestam contra illusores sacrorum Dei vindicis præsentiam testatum. Hoc miraculum jam tertijs literis esse confirmatum. In mendacium calidissimum anno sequente calamum strinxerat ὁ μακαρίτης Cl. Hottingerus noster. Sed fabulam eam alia eáque centumcubitali, publicis novellis ijdem Jesuitæ hoc ipso anno interpolárunt & auxerunt. Recitabimus totidem Novellarum verba: Sæviente Tiguri lue epidemica & urbem fœdum depopulante, plures é civibus præcisa spe medicorum confugerunt ad aram Deiparæ virginisacram, nec frustra. Plurimi enim implorata Divæ virginis opera & votis eidem litatis suam, quâ periclitabantur, recepere valetudinem. Cujus rei obstupescendæ fama universam urbem & viciniam pervasit. Secundum alios autem quidam prædicans ex umbone, hac rei novitate & miraculo commotus, in conferta hominum multitudine, in Deiparæ virginis commendationem linguam laxavit. Res hæc delata est ad Magistratum, decretúmque, ut coram eadem populi corona, quâ hæc figmenta venum protrusisset, palinodiam caneret. Quo senatus mandato percepto, Prædicans tantùm abfuit, ut temperârit, quin potiùs suos in cœpta & continuanta erga Deiparam virginem devotione multó ferventiús excitárit. Quapropter in vincula conjectus, propositis minis & pœnis gravissimis jussus á susceptamente decedere, à qua tamen ille ne latum unguem deflexit, imó judicibus coram Zwinglium cum suis erroribus & blasphemijs, execrabatur, palam dicens, voce quantâ posset maximâ, solam Romanam fidem esse verum ovile Christi, & unam ad æternam salutem januam. Judices cùm adverterent, se oleum in hoc homine ad priorem mentem reducendo & operam perdere, Prædicantem ut hæreticum & Patriæ conturbatorem mortis damnant. Deducitur itaque ad ferale pegma & locum supplicij, urbe tota confluente. Ipse verò hilari vultu gradiebatur, proximos quosvis ad Deiparæ virginis cultum & Romanam fidem suscipiendam adhortans, summásque Deo & magnæ Matri grates agens, quód pro vera fide propaganda liceat sibi vitam & animam ponere. Cùm ad locum supplicij perventum est, nullo signo formidinis, vultu lœto, spectatoribus omnibus stupentibus & illachrymantibus, fatalem carnificis ictum excepit. Tum verò carnifex interrogabat pro more in Helvetia recepto judicem, utrum huic reo Catholico secundum jura & leges Patriae caput a cervice resecuisset? Cui judex concitatiore voce & animo respondit, eum non Catholico sed haretico impiam animam extorsisse. Vix haec effatus, ecce tibi! multitudine tota spectante truncus & caput tertio motus vitales exeruit. Hocce spectaculo attonitus & motus adeo carnisex & triginta alij spectatores, ut palam exclamarint, hominem eum sanctum esse, & eam solam orthodoxam fidem, quam hic vitae & sanguinis sui profusione comprobasset. Quis non lecta tam speciosa, tam exquisita narratione publica luce donata, induceretur, ut rem ita gestam esse crederet? Te vero, Redingi, per omnia sacra imploramus testem, an tale quid vel fando & per transennam unquam audiveris? Vicinus es enim nobis, & sunt inter tuos, qui quotidie oras nostras frequentent, quos nihil eorum, quae publica in luce & conspectu geruntur, latere potest. Et tamen portentosa haec & Antichristiana mendacia, quae ne ipse quidem Sathanas affabre magis construeret & architectaretur, non tantum in Italia, Hispania & extremis Jesuitarum oris authentica habebuntur, sed etiam ex Jesuitarum novellis in annales relata posteritate glisicent. Quis igitur sanus vestra magis magisque, quae ad ravim usque insani decantatis, miracula non detestabitur? Quis ea non adscribet miraculis Antichristi, de quibus consignatissimam habemus Prophetiam ad postrema tempora pertinentem 2. Thess 2:9?
units.tr: Still, I cannot refrain from setting before you, as a specimen, two most recent prodigious lies [ψευδῆ τέρατα], as many miracles, which have been most impudently published in Cologne in the Jesuits' recent news-sheets, supposedly performed in this very city of Zurich, our beloved homeland, to establish the Papist doctrine. As for the first, five years have passed since the Latin news-sheets printed by the Jesuit authors at Cologne, and published, reported that a certain Catholic (a Papist, that is) came to Zurich and, seized by a sudden sickness, ordered a Catholic priest to be summoned, to whom he might confess his sins and from whom he might be furnished with viaticum for his last journey. When the sick man's request was conveyed to a heretic babbler (who had previously been orthodox), the staged comedy was soon to turn into a tragedy. Admitted to the sick man, he heard his confession and, with a feigned Roman rite, absolved him. Then he was ordered to offer the holy viaticum; he produced a little piece of bread, and he was already about to make a mockery of the sick man in this way, when the door of the bedroom was knocked upon, and he was ordered to wait outside, while the knocking was heard, until the scene was finished. But the knocker insisted more boldly on knocking again, and when he had knocked a third time, without waiting for permission to enter, he opened the door, and seized the preacher, who was thinking of nothing less, together with his piece of bread, leaving no trace of him behind. The wretched man is still missing, and by his absence he bore witness to the manifest presence of the avenger of God's sacred things against the mockers. This miracle has now been confirmed by third letters. The late Hottinger, our distinguished colleague, took up his pen against this very hot lie in the following year. But the same Jesuits have this year embellished and enlarged that tale with another, and an even more far-fetched one, in their public news-sheets. We shall quote the very words of the news-sheets: While a plague was raging at Zurich and foully depopulating the city, many of the citizens, their hope of physicians cut off, fled to the altar of the Mother of God, the Virgin, and not in vain. For very many, having implored the aid of the divine Virgin and offered vows to her, recovered the health which they had been losing. The report of this astonishing thing spread through the whole city and its neighbourhood. According to others, a certain preacher, moved by this novelty and miracle, loosed his tongue in praise of the Mother of God in the crowded multitude of people from his pulpit. The matter was reported to the Magistrate, and it was decreed that he should sing a palinode before the same crowd of people before whom he had put these fictions on sale. When the Senate's order was received, the preacher was so far from restraining himself that he rather stirred up his followers to an even more fervent devotion in the course and continuance of their devotion to the Virgin Mother of God. Therefore, he was thrown into chains, and, with threats and most severe penalties set before him, was ordered to desist from that devotion, from which he did not bend a hair's breadth. Nay, in the presence of the judges he execrated Zwingli with his errors and blasphemies, openly saying, with the loudest voice he could, that the Roman faith alone is the true fold of Christ and the one gate to eternal salvation. When the judges perceived that they were wasting their effort and oil in trying to lead this man back to his former mind, they condemned the preacher to death as a heretic and a troubler of the fatherland. He was therefore led to the fatal scaffold and the place of punishment, with the whole city flocking together. He himself walked with a cheerful countenance, exhorting all who were near him to the worship of the Virgin Mother of God and to the acceptance of the Roman faith, and giving the highest thanks to God and the great Mother that it was permitted him to lay down his life and soul for the propagation of the true faith. When they came to the place of punishment, with no sign of fear, with a joyful countenance, while all the spectators stood amazed and wept, he received the fatal blow of the executioner. Then the executioner, according to the custom received in Helvetia, asked the judge whether he had cut off the head of this Catholic prisoner according to the laws and statutes of the fatherland. The judge replied in a louder voice and with a more excited spirit that he had not dispatched a Catholic but an impious heretic. Scarcely had he spoken, when, lo! with the whole crowd watching, the trunk and the head moved three times and gave signs of life. Astonished and moved by this spectacle, the executioner and thirty other spectators cried out that the man was holy, and that the only orthodox faith was the one which he had confirmed by the pouring out of his blood and life. Who, having read so specious and exquisite a narrative, published to the light of day, would not be led to believe that the matter had happened in this way? But you, Reding, we implore by all that is sacred to be our witness: have you ever heard anything of this kind, even by rumour or in passing? For you are our neighbour, and among your people there are those who visit our shores every day, and nothing that is done in the public light and view can be hidden from them. And yet these portentous and Antichristian lies, which Satan himself could not have fashioned and contrived more skilfully, will be held authentic not only in Italy, Spain and the farthest outposts of the Jesuits, but will also, once carried from the Jesuits' news-sheets into the annals, be spread abroad for posterity. Who, then, that is sane, would not detest the miracles which you, insane, chant again and again until you are hoarse? Who would not ascribe them to the miracles of Antichrist, of which we have a most clearly attested prophecy, relating to the last times, 2 Thess. 2:9?

units.la: XXVIII. De miraculis porro Redingius allegat sententiam Philippi Melanchthonis in cap.3. Matthaei ejusmodi: Quando magnae sunt tenebrae, vocari novos Doctores, & semper addi a Deo miracula, ut sciamus a Deo esse missos.
units.tr: XXVIII. Further, on the subject of miracles, Redingius cites a saying of Philip Melanchthon on Matthew 3, to this effect: When darkness is great, new teachers are called, and God always adds miracles, so that we may know they have been sent by God.

units.la: Subsumit autem: Numquid circa Reformationem erant tenebrae, dum teste Breitingero, Opusculo de sectis, mille sexaginta annis ita de medio hominum perijt, ut esset incognita & abscondita? Annon igitur miraculis opus erat, ut in lucem produceretur a Zwinglio ejusque sectatoribus? pag.189. At quas tenebras intellexerit Melanchthon, adversario expendendum fuerat.
units.tr: He then argues: Was there not darkness around the Reformation, when, according to Breitinger in his Opusculum de sectis, for a thousand and sixty years the truth had so disappeared from among men that it was unknown and hidden? Was there not therefore a need for miracles, so that it might be brought into the light by Zwingli and his followers? p. 189. But what darkness Melanchthon meant should have been examined by the opponent.

units.la: Tales nempe intelligit, quæ luci seu Evangelio jam ante prædicato locum nullum relinquunt. Agit enim de miraculis Johannis Baptistæ tempore patratis. At tum Evangelium nec prædicatum nec plantatum fuerat. Novus Ecclesiæ status induci debuit. Miraculis igitur opus erat.
